# I, Frankenstein — Kindle working manuscript

Generated from story.html. Conventions:

- The reader keeps two scores, **Empathy** and **Alienation**, both starting at 0. Instructions to change them appear as `> Add 1 to your Empathy score.`

- Every true/false flag in the game is a **keyword** the reader notes down. Placeholders are `KW_<name>`; rename them as you like. `> Note the keyword KW_x.` means the reader writes it down; `> Delete the keyword` means they cross it out.

- The third score, Trust, is not tracked by the reader. Instead each section that depends on it exists in several numbered copies, one per **Trust thread** (shown in the page header). Links always send the reader to the copy that matches their choices, so the reader never sees Trust.

- Text that today appears only under a condition is marked `[[If you have KW_x, read the following:]]` when it is a whole paragraph, or `[[!! EDIT inline, if …: …]]` when it sits inside a sentence. **Every !! EDIT marker needs your hand**: decide whether to keep both readings with a keyword instruction, or rewrite the sentence so one wording serves both.

- Choices are listed as `• text — turn to N`. A choice shown only under a condition is prefixed `[If …]`. A `→ If …, turn to N` line is an automatic continuation that depends on a keyword or score.

- 2933 numbered pages and 141 keyword placeholders. 3724 !! EDIT markers in all, but only 980 distinct edit sites: the rest are the same sentence repeated in Trust-thread copies, so fix it once and paste the fix into the other copies.

- Copies of a section in different Trust threads have identical text and instructions except where the page carries a `!! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT` note; otherwise only the link numbers differ.

# PART ONE — 'I BEGIN THE CREATION OF A HUMAN BEING'

## 1
*(01_01)*

[ILLUSTRATION: pic1_1.jpg]

*...the ethereal energy
which wise Prometheus temper'd into paste
And, mixt with living streams, the godlike image cast.
From such rude principles our form began;
And earth was metamophos'd into man.*

**CHAPTER ONE**
*The Workshop of Filthy Creation*

It was quieter in Paris today, though the riots have left scars. Half the ground-floor windows have boards over broken panes and there are holes in the street where cobblestones have been gouged up to use as missiles. After a night in the library I made my way home by the Place Maubert, in hope the baker would have macaroons again, but his shutters were closed, drips of fresh paint proclaiming his pride in the tricolour. It could merely be a ploy to avoid having his shop ransacked, I suppose, but everywhere now you will see such displays of revolutionary fervour.

I'm on my way back to my lodgings. Will you walk with me?

• Yes. — turn to 2

## 2
*(01_02)*

We can cut through these back streets. It's not even ten minutes' walk from here. Or perhaps you would prefer the scenic route?

• The short cut is fine. — turn to 3
• By all means let's see the sights. — turn to 4

## 3
*(01_03)*

That's better. I love following these narrow alleys. You can emerge half a mile from where you set out and it's as if you've burrowed through space and time. And, of course, it's a relief to get away from the teeming crowds. Just keep your wits about you. While the law is busy rounding up aristocrats, common thieves have been flourishing.

What were we talking about? Ah yes, macaroons. There was a crowd outside the store, mostly women with empty baskets. They must have known the bakery would not open today, but it gives them a place to talk. And these are days when there is much to talk about. It is as though the air carries a charge, a vital spark that forces the heart to beat quicker. And the haze over the city now that autumn is here - dust from all the crowds, of course, but shining like the golden clouds that shroud Olympus.

A girl caught my arm. She had a tray of cockades, knots of cheap gaudy ribbons on a pin. 'Every citizen must wear one,' she said, and her eyes were so wide and bright. Hope and fear... Which is at the forefront, I wonder?

• People are excited by the future — turn to 5
• People are anxious — turn to 6

## 4
*(01_04)*

Well now, if you're new to Paris, there's a sight for you: the Panthéon. An extraordinary tomb, is it not, all for one man? The statesman Mirabeau is buried there. A hundred thousand tonnes of stone to proclaim what any child can write as enduringly with a knife in the bark of a tree: "I was here". That's how much men fear, not death, but being forgotten.

What were we talking about? Ah yes, macaroons. There was a crowd outside the store, mostly women with empty baskets. They must have known the bakery would not open today, but it gives them a place to talk. And these are days when there is much to talk about. It is as though the air carries a charge, a vital spark that forces the heart to beat quicker. And the haze over the city now that autumn is here - dust from all the crowds, of course, but shining like the golden clouds that shroud Olympus.

A girl caught my arm. She had a tray of cockades, knots of cheap gaudy ribbons on a pin. 'Every citizen must wear one,' she said, and her eyes were so wide and bright. Hope and fear... Which is at the forefront, I wonder?

• People are excited by the future — turn to 5
• People are anxious — turn to 6

## 5
*(01_06)*

Yes, I feel it too. What a time to be alive! All of history to this moment has been lived in the childhood of Mankind, and now we have come to childhood's end. For there is no natural law that places one man on a throne and another at his feet. Such an order is the grossest violation of natural law, where the only true authority flows from reason. The people have arrested their tyrant, and now they have the power to shape their own future. That look in their eyes - it is the same excitement I felt when, stepping from the carriage that brought me from Geneva four years ago, I first stood before the university gates. That's why I bought the cockade even though - look, the ghastly cheap thing has already come unravelled.

• What is your name? — turn to 9

## 6
*(01_07)*

No doubt you are right. I see the mirror of my own feelings in everyone I pass, their eyes shining with hope and fear - for the one always contains the other. You could never mistake it for the sleepy amiability of my native Geneva.

• These are dangerous times — turn to 8
• What is your name? — turn to 9
• It would be better if you went home — turn to 7

## 7
*(01_08)*

I see you are unfamiliar with life in Geneva. It is all very fine if you are a cow with a bell about its neck - or a well-fed merchant, which amounts to much the same. Yet the future is a coming storm, and whether we go out to confront it boldly, or hide behind our shutters, it will sweep over us just the same. These people of Paris who pass by us - yes, there is fear in their eyes. But courage too. Their Revolution is a flame that will set the world alight - Geneva too - and from the ashes a new and better era will rise. I passionately believe that. It is the precept that has guided my studies from the mire of medievalism towards the shining city on the hill.

• What is your name? — turn to 9

## 8
*(01_09)*

You must understand that here the people have suffered under the most appalling tyranny. It is not so long ago that philosophers were burned alive with their books, at the decree of an absolute monarch whose whims were as irresistible as death. A man might starve for want of a crust of bread, while another could choose to keep eating until he was sick.

And now the royal family has been seized by the mob, and all Europe is in outcry. But you should see it simply as a chemical reaction that had long been out of equilibrium. In restoring it to a placid state, reagents have been added that swing it the other way - unshaven guards outside the Tuileries, men who cannot read or write appointed as court judges. Yes, there are riots. It is the unknown that lies ahead, and the unknown is what men fear. But I have confidence that reason will prevail. It must. Men are not animals.

• What is your name? — turn to 9

## 9
*(01_0A)*

Why, what a question. Surely you know me?

• Of course, you are Baron Frankenstein. — turn to 10

## 10
*(01_0B)*

Baron? I am no aristocrat! Just plain Victor Frankenstein, the son of a Geneva magistrate. Our family is respected and I daresay we are more fortunate than most, but we are hardly noblemen. Which is just as well, since the National Assembly has abolished the nobility and even the Duke of Orléans nowadays styles himself 'Citizen Philip Equality'.

• A brave new world! — turn to 11
• The mob drags everyone down to their level — turn to 12
• What about your family? — turn to 15

## 11
*(01_0C)*

Indeed. Let me ask you something, my friend. What are the greatest accomplishments of Man? We could list the cathedral at Chartres, the Sistine Chapel, Allegri's *Miserere*. But all of these great works are tarnished, in my eyes, for they do not advance understanding. They merely celebrate what already is - and that celebration, not of the glory of Man, but of myth.

Now consider the events that are sweeping across the world. A spirit of confidence, optimism, bold enquiry. Men *dare* now. In my own endeavours, I seek discoveries as revolutionary as those of Copernicus and Columbus. It [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_louis_capet: is]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_louis_capet: *is*]] a new world - a time in which mankind can storm the gates of Eden and take for ourselves a seat in paradise. You quoted Shakespeare - let me assure you, I will 'wake the sleepers with my so potent art'.

But the thoroughfare is not the place to discuss matters of such weight. See, I allowed my words to become heated and a crowd gathers. Later, later.

• Let's talk about something else. — turn to 15
• What sleepers? Who would you wake? — turn to 13

## 12
*(01_0D)*

> Note the keyword KW_louis_capet.

See those guardsmen in their red liberty caps? How they would scowl if you spoke to them of 'the King'. To them he is now simply Citizen Louis Capet - or perhaps 'Louis the Last'. But I ask you, how can a man of any worth be lessened by stripping away titles and signs of rank and privilege? They are just tokens, they don't define a person. Could you not equally say that the Revolution ennobles all of us? What a man makes of himself can now be determined by his nature, not by the accident of birth.

• 'Not in our stars, but in ourselves'? — turn to 11
• And what accident of birth have you escaped? — turn to 15

## 13
*(01_0E)*

You may have heard Citizen Fouché's favourite dictum, 'Death is an eternal sleep'? No? Well, in any case I was speaking figuratively. The dissecting room and the charnel house supply many of my materials, but my goal is not to bring the dead to life. It is - But no, not here. Later I will show you.

• You seem very agitated. — turn to 14
• How long have you been engaged in your work? — turn to 15

## 14
*(01_0F)*

Yes, I have been working very hard, perhaps too hard. See this letter my father sent? Here: 'I know that while you are pleased, you will think of us with affection. You must pardon me if I regard any interruption in your correspondence as evidence that your other duties -' Duties, he says. ' - your other duties are equally neglected.'

*Mens sana in corpore sano*, he means. How well he knows me. I am by nature inclined to an excess of zeal that can harm my health. But my *duties!* He has no idea!

I must write to him. And Elizabeth. Henri too. I'll do it tonight. I cannot tell them of my work - not until I am certain of success. You know, it's strange that I came to Paris at this very time. It's as though the world has woken up around me, as though the great endeavour to which I have set myself has inspired a general casting-off of superstition. Coincidence, naturally. ## 16
*(01_0H)*

> Note the keyword KW_victor_describes_elizabeth.

My father's sister married an Italian gentleman. Soon after the wedding, they moved to Italy, and for some years my father had very little communication with her. She died when I was four years old, and her husband wrote to my father to say that he intended to remarry. 'It is my wish,' he said, 'that you should take charge of the infant, and raise her as your own daughter. Her mother's fortune is secured to her. Reflect upon this proposition and decide whether you would prefer educating your niece yourself to her being brought up by a stepmother.'

My father did not hesitate, and immediately went to Italy, to fetch the little Elizabeth Lavenza home. I often heard my late mother say that she was the most beautiful child she had ever seen, and showed signs even then of a gentle and affectionate disposition. These indications, and a desire to bind the ties of domestic love, determined my mother to consider Elizabeth as my future wife; a design which she never found reason to repent.

## 17

She caught the scarlet fever from Elizabeth. It was just before I was due to start my first term at university. I don't know if you have lost anyone close to you. It is a long time before you can accept that the person whose very existence appeared a part of your own is gone forever. You know it in your mind to be true, but on some level it is beyond understanding. And time, they say, eases grief, but my experience is that it sharpens it. When finally we realize we will never see the beloved face again, the full bitter weight of grief bears down on us.

But where is the sense in me telling you about a sorrow which all have felt, and must feel? The time comes when grief is an indulgence rather than a necessity, and we have lives to live and duties to perform. My mother's dying wish was that Elizabeth and I should one day marry, and so we shall - when my work is complete.

## 21
*(01_0M)*

Science gripped my imagination from an early age. In other studies you go as far as others have gone before you, and there is nothing more to know; but in a scientific pursuit there is continual discovery, continual wonder. So it was with me throughout my first two years of study here in Paris. My insatiable thirst for learning astonished my fellow students, and my proficiency soon impressed the masters.

When I realized that my professors could teach me no more - indeed, that in my grasp of the landscape yet undiscovered I could see more clearly than they - I thought of returning home to Geneva, to my friends and family. Then an incident happened that led me onto a fresh course of study, and that has protracted my stay these last two years.

## 22
*(01_0N)*

> Add 1 to your Empathy score.

My rooms are in the Rue Mouffetard, and meals are brought in by an old servant. Often I forget the time, however, and turn from my work to find the bread stale or the soup gone cold. Thus I will often be found breakfasting in a tavern on the way to lectures, a book propped open in one hand as I cram in food along with knowledge.

On the day I'm speaking of, the back room of the tavern was undergoing repairs when suddenly there was a great shout and the din of chisels stopped. Distracted more by the whispers of the workmen than I had been by their singing moments earlier, I went to see what was happening. The room was thick with mortar dust and chips of brick and stone lay everywhere. They had not put out sheets for some reason, so the table and chairs where I had often sat debating with my fellow students now seemed as a ruin long abandoned to time. On the table lay an object which I perceived to be a mummified human hand. A workman had found it behind the brickwork of the chimney.

I have no idea how it came to be there. That was not the mystery that occupied my interest. Rather it was the length of the nails, which are often said to grow after death. The sight of that hand, of unknown age and origin, severed and sealed away for who knows what reason, and yet continuing for a time to nurture some flickering spark of the essence of life … That is the question that has burned like a beacon before me these last two years. What is the essence of life, and how may it be generated?

• And you have found the answer? — turn to 25

## 23
*(01_0O)*

> Note the keyword KW_dissecting_room_and_charnel_house.

I have always been fascinated by the structure of the human body, or indeed of any animal. Behold, a manikin of fleshy clay binding up an interior of hard calcium and liquid-filled tubes. A machine - and yet it breathes, the heart drives the blood, and that heart quickens in response to fear or anger or love. Emotions - they were not on the list of ingredients. So where do they come from? Where does the principle of life originate? The ghost in the machine - that is what I desired to have under my microscope.

Soon after arriving at the university, I began to focus my studies on biology and physiology. But where those studies took me was on a foul journey indeed. If I had not been so driven to penetrate the mystery, I would soon have abandoned it. You see, I had not only to become acquainted with the surgeon's saw and scalpel. It was also necessary for me to scour the slaughterhouses and dissecting rooms for choice items as avidly as other students search the shelves of bookshops. I collected bones from charnel houses. On wooden frames, such as my beloved Elizabeth would use to practice needlework, I decanted serums of bodily fluids and grew tissue cultures on dishes all around my room. I stretched flesh in varying stages of putrefaction, the better to understand what processes are held in check by the force we call life.

I was about fifteen years old. We were at our house near Belrive and there was a massive thunderstorm. It swept down from behind the mountains of Jura, and the thunder burst directly overhead with a violence that made the plates rattle on the dresser.

The whole time the storm lasted, I stood at the door watching its progress with curiosity and delight. Suddenly I saw a stream of fire issue from an old and beautiful oak which stood about twenty yards from our house; and so soon as the dazzling light vanished, the oak had disappeared, and nothing remained but a blasted stump.

## 95
*(01_2P)*

A young woman in the bloom of health calls to me across the street. It's Elizabeth[[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_victor_describes_elizabeth: , my cousin]]. Surprised to see her here in Paris, and filled with delight, I run to embrace her. She draws me back into the doorway of an abandoned shop, on which the old seals that used to be used in times of plague can be seen peeling. I cradle her sweet face tenderly, realizing how I have missed her.

'No one will see us here,' she says with a smile that shows her teeth, and she presses against me. The fabric of her dress is very thin. I feel the heat of her body. As we kiss, I feel her tongue probe my lips. My heart is pounding. Her tongue in my mouth is cold, so cold, and I pull away, suddenly afraid. There is a smell in the air - her perfume, yes, but behind that a taint of things locked away for a long time.

This is not Elizabeth. It is my dead mother's head that I hold in my hands, the neck sliced raggedly, the eyes opaque as mothballs. Maggots crawl out from between her livid lips, from her nose, from the torn hole of her windpipe. And as they fall they burst on the flagstones, tiny stars of blood patterning the ground.

Such depraved ideas! I can't think of Elizabeth in that way. Oh no, I'm not fit to hold her now. Hands that have done the filthy work of last night - I could never wash them clean enough to deserve a pure being such as she.

Was that what Coleridge envisaged when he spoke of the frightful fiend that 'doth close behind him tread'? Fear and dread indeed! I never knew those emotions till now. Oh God, I feel sick with them.

Here's the inn where the carriages stop. What impulse brought me here? No mystery - it's the urge to get away. To go home, forget everything that has happened here. I curse the day I first opened a book, as it brought me to the vilest and most blasphemous act any man has ever done. Yes, I should buy a ticket to Geneva right now. My things can be sent on. I can wait no longer. I pour it all out. The inspiration which fixed the terrible, burning idea in my head. The long hours - days, weeks, months - in which I laboured to construct a frame for the reception of life. The thousand setbacks that threw me back to the bottom of the precipice and the long climb back each time. The midnight toil in which, tense and unbreathing, I pursued nature to her hiding places. The scrape of spade on grave soil, scalpel on flesh, hacksaw on bone. I tell him of the crack as the switch closed, the acrid smell of electricity, the rasp of artificial lungs tasting air for the first time.

'Imagine it, Henri! The sound of [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its own blood racing in stolen veins is all it knows, having come into the world by way of rifled graves and dissecting trays instead of the womb. In alembics like this it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his own blood racing in stolen veins is all he knows, having come into the world by way of rifled graves and dissecting trays instead of the womb. In alembics like this he]] was born. What a moment! When Herschel found his new planet, that was not a tenth so momentous. I can give life. Perhaps even reverse death.'

I want so much for Henri to understand. He above all. But the look in his eyes is not wonder. It is a reflection of what I feel for myself. Pity.

'Will you pour the coffee, Henri? I can't sit. I'm too excited.'

'What's wrong, Victor? You don't seem yourself. I'm glad my arrival here has pleased you, but - '

'It's not only that. My skin is tingling - every nerve ending, so sensitive. I feel everything. The roughness of the napkin. The fragility of this china. Oh, it's too delicate. I'll break it.'

'Your hand is shaking. Victor, I think you have a fever.'

'What? No. Hah, are you the doctor now, Henri? I can't stay still. There's so much going on, outside and in. Look at those children down there. They have a splendid kite. Remember - ha ha! We used to fly our kite at Lake Murten. Do you remember?'

'My dear Victor, what, for God's sake, is the matter? Don't laugh in that manner. How ill you are! What is the cause of all this?'

'Don't ask me. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: *It* can tell. See it?]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: *He* can tell. See him?]]Banquo with his flesh all stripped away!'

'You think I'm mad. Don't lie, Henri. I can see it in your eyes.'

Look at those children down there. That's a splendid kite they've got. Remember when we used to fly our kite at Lake Murten. Do you remember, Henri?'

## 121
*(01_3F)*

I can see Henri's face looking down at me. He's saying something. I can hear him, I can feel his grip as he shakes me, but it doesn't seem to matter now. Nothing matters.

I had passion without compassion. Logic to see my way to the summit, but not the imagination or the empathy to understand what it would mean to stand there, breathless, under the uncaring sky.

When my creature opened its eyes, that was the moment I had worked for unceasingly every day for two years. It had never been out of my thoughts in all that time, and yet it took me by surprise. I had never considered the feelings it would awaken. I had made a fatal miscalculation. Into all my precisely calculated equations, I failed to factor myself.

Now you can see faces bobbing and swaying above the hedgerows - but not living faces, the slack and vacant expressions of dead men. They are severed heads, white and blood-flecked, mounted on sharp poles that the leaders of the crowd are brandishing with triumphal glee.

As the procession comes into view around the hedges you see most of them are armed with clubs and knives, and a few with sticks that they use to send volleys of fire and smoke up into the air. It was the cracking of those fire-sticks that woke you.

There are far too many to fight. Luckily they seem unaware of you. They go marching past, jeering and laughing and screaming. There are hundreds of them and it seems to take forever, but finally the last straggler vanishes along the road.

The young man returns with a basket full of firewood across his shoulders. Taking the young woman aside, he shows her a parcel he has with him containing a small loaf and a piece of cheese. You crawl out of your hovel and under the bushes where you can get a better look.

They pass so close you could reach out and touch them, and at that moment your heart catches in your throat. You have never had the opportunity before for such quiet contemplation of your fellow man. The younger man is slim and graceful, the look on his face one of careful attention to his companion, who holds onto his arm for support.

They are huddled up in thicker clothes than your own scant covering. Their cheeks burn with bright pink spots and their breath makes ragged white puffs in the declining light of the sun. It drifts towards your hiding place and you could breathe it in - the very air from their lungs. They must feel the cold, but still they are enjoying the serenity of the closing day. ## 192

Felix is often sad. Perhaps that's why you feel the greatest kinship with him. Often you see him coming in from the fields with a frown on his handsome face and shoulders bowed as though under a terrible burden. It seems as if each step costs him all his energy, and he would like to throw himself to the ground and never move again. ## 193
*(01_5M)*

A thaw sets in as the days start to become noticeably longer. One morning, you are cupping your hands to drink from a pond when a shaft of sunlight hits your face, which appears with fiery clarity in the water.

Of course you've seen your reflection before. But this time it comes as a shock. You are so used to spending the day watching the family that you have come to fancy yourself as one of them. The red, gristly countenance with the round yellow eyes and skeletal grimace is like some creature of the depths staring up at you from the water. You feel a thrill of fear, as if it might reach up and drag you down into a mire of darkness from which there is no escape.

You scurry back thirsty to your lair, pulling the twigs and leaves behind you as if that might shut out the scrutiny of some immense, unseen, celestial eye that is somehow judging you. And if such an eye exists, what does it make of you?

• That you are hideously ugly? — turn to 194

## 194
*(01_5N)*

You are. More than ugly: monstrous. Even the cat has taken to slinking out of your small store of food if it sees you approaching, and will not suffer to let you stroke it, though it stretches contentedly enough in Agatha's lap.

The thought of Agatha's caresses makes you press your fists to your temples to squeeze out those feelings that can only torture you. She would never greet you with smiles and soothing words, or run light fingers over your aching limbs.

Why is Felix sad? Why are your family so poor? They begin to obsess your sleeping hours as well as your attention while awake. In your dreams, you don't peer in through a crack in the wall, you sit among them in the parlour. As they talk of their sorrows, though their language remains a clash of meaningless sounds, in the dream you listen judiciously, with profound understanding, weighing every thought as they sit watching you with eager smiles. Your gentle demeanour and wisdom have entirely won their favour - no, even their love - so that they do not see you as a monster but as their saviour who has come to protect them and restore their happiness.

You wake to see the buds on the trees are turning to blossom. The din of birdsong fills the air, dew sparkles on the grass where only a week ago lay snow, and the scent of flowers is woken by a sun returning joy to the world after the long, long months of winter. But how do you feel?

• Are you hopeful? — turn to 196
• Or fearful? — turn to 197

## 195
*(01_5O)*

Your appearance sets you apart, it's true. Yet inside you have the same feelings, the same needs. Your stomach rumbles at the smell of baking bread or a ripe cheese. If you cut yourself, you make the same noise as Felix does, the same reflex of jerking back the injured hand, of putting your tongue over the cut. You feel pain in the same way - so why not sadness and joy and love? You are a man like him. But unkind nature has made you in such a way that no one can see that.

Why is Felix sad? Why are your family so poor? They begin to obsess your sleeping hours as well as your attention while awake. In your dreams, you don't peer in through a crack in the wall, you sit among them in the parlour. As they talk of their sorrows, though their language remains a clash of meaningless sounds, in the dream you listen judiciously, with profound understanding, weighing every thought as they sit watching you with eager smiles. Your gentle demeanour and wisdom have entirely won their favour - no, even their love - so that they do not see you as a monster but as their saviour who has come to protect them and restore their happiness.

You wake to see the buds on the trees are turning to blossom. The din of birdsong fills the air, dew sparkles on the grass where only a week ago lay snow, and the scent of flowers is woken by a sun returning joy to the world after the long, long months of winter. But how do you feel?

## 198
*(01_5S)*

With spring comes warmth, and pleasant sprinkling showers that rapidly transform the earth. The family spent the winter months huddled close to the fire whenever tasks did not force them outside, but now they live mostly in the open air. Father quits his parlour to sit out on the lawn for several hours each day. Even Felix, as he sets off to work in the fields, now walks with a less mournful trudge.

The birds sing more cheerful notes. The leaves bud forth on the trees. Happy, happy earth! A fit habitation for gods now, though a short time ago it was bleak, damp, and unwholesome. Your spirits are elevated by the enchanting appearance of nature. The past is blotted from your memory. The present is tranquil, and - at least in your most optimistic moments - the future is gilded by bright rays of hope.

The season advances rapidly. The weather is fine, the skies cloudless. The nights when you are abroad foraging are balmy, and you come back to your home laden with fruit. It astonishes you that what before was barren should now bloom with the most beautiful flowers and greenery. Each day brings a thousand scents of delight and a thousand sights of beauty.

And then, one morning, a newcomer arrives whose presence will work the magic of spring on your little family.

One night, while foraging in the wood, you venture further than usual and come upon a road. On the far side, the ground slopes steeply away towards a surging river. You stand for a moment enjoying the sensation of overlooking the tops of the mighty pines, which you are used to seeing soar high up on all sides high above you. The sky is already getting lighter, and you are just about to head back to your lair when you notice a leather trunk in the ditch beside the road. A broken rope lies beside it, by which you gather it must have fallen from one of the coaches you have seen only from afar.

It is locked, but you quickly break the hasp. What a treasure trove! There is a thick cloak, along with shirts and fabric with which you should be able to make yourself good clothing before the winter. And beneath that you find a still greater prize: several books.

Back in the hovel, you investigate your find. Some are written in a language you don't know, but there are three you can decipher. They are John Milton's *Paradise Lost*, a volume of Plutarch's *Lives of the Noble Greeks and Romans*, and *Travels* by Thomas Jefferson. Now you can study and improve your mind throughout the day, without having to wait for Safiye's next lesson.

The book comprises short biographies of men who, you gather, lived long ago and did great deeds, governing ancient republics on which the precepts of liberty and equality are founded. Plutarch's writings elevate you above the wretchedness of your own condition as your imagination carries you among the admirable heroes of past ages. You feel sure that Pyrrhus would have welcomed you among the ranks of his companions, that Cato would have perceived in you an integrity to match his own, that the Spartans would have admired your fortitude and the Athenians your dedication to acquiring wisdom.

Plutarch intended a lesson in juxtaposing these lives. Some of the men he describes dedicate their lives to great works and public affairs, others to massacring or enslaving their species. Your studies have equipped you with a sophisticated mind, so the lesson does not escape your notice, but to which kind of story are you most drawn?

## 242

It is the journal of Victor Frankenstein. In it he describes the months that led up to your inception, minutely setting out every step he took in the progress of his work. It is no story of divine creation. No clay became flesh by the agency of thunderbolt or blazing sun. Instead you are forced by self-torturing curiosity to read the whole series of disgusting circumstances that produced a misshapen golem of reconstructed flesh and assembled parts. The minutest description of your odious and loathsome creation is given, in language which vividly paints your maker's horrors and renders yours indelible. You feel sick but you cannot tear your eyes away.

'Hateful day when I received life!' you groan in agony. 'Cursed creator! Why did you form a monster so hideous that even you turned from me in disgust? God, in pity, made Man beautiful and alluring, after his own image. But my form is a filthy type of yours, more horrid from its very resemblance. Satan had his companions, fellow-devils, to admire and encourage him, but I am solitary and detested.'

## 317
*(01_9C)*

Nature decays around you and the sun is drained of heat. Rain and snow gust out of grey skies. Lakes and rivers are frozen. The surface of the earth becomes hard and chill and bare. Across empty windswept fields you watch the warm lights of cottages with envy, and the few times you creep into a village by night you make sure to help yourself to food from the meanest homes, so that the deprivation will be more keenly felt. For why should babies be snug in cradles, and their parents sup heartily by a warm fire, while you are fated to haunt the drizzle and the lonely hedgerows?

At long last you begin to perceive that the blue hump on the horizon is not cloud, but the rise of land into the mountains around Geneva. Daily it comes closer. At the same time, the days are growing longer and warmer, the grass is greener. A new year is coming to life. The year in which you will confront your maker.

You have his notebook still. Would it be wise to look inside and see what you can learn before your meeting with him? And yet - the account of your creation, phrased in so glacially aloof a tone, reducing the marvel of your existence to so many millilitres of this, a certain number of grafts and sutures, like the recipe for an ammoniacal stew. It is hard to bear.

[ILLUSTRATION: pic3_1.jpg]

*you wild winds, thus can you sleep so still

**CHAPTER ONE**
*Even Cato Wept*

Snowflakes are drifting past the window. For a time they become confused in my mind with the peeling paint on the shutters. A curl of white trembles in the breeze, vibrating with an awful anxiety, fragile yet never quite breaking free. That flake of paint is both familiar to me and very dreadful. I am conscious as I continue to watch it that I have been a stranger to the world for weeks. Perhaps months.

Hearing a commotion in the street, shouts and a burst of raucous song, I ask Henri if it is New Year.

'The year starts when the government says,' he replies without turning from the window. The reply is almost a reflex, as though speaking to himself, and from his tone I gather he has grown used to me sliding away into a state of extreme detachment.

I sit upright in the chair. 'How long have I been ill, Henri?'

It takes him a moment to respond. He slowly looks round at me, and the lines of weariness melt away as his face lights up. 'Victor!'

## 337
*(01_9Y)*

By slow degrees my recovery continues over the following weeks. True, there are relapses, usually on dull days when the view from the window is grey and rain spits against the panes. Then I sit for hours staring at my boots beside the door or the pattern on the china, feeling that slow horror of familiar things that creeps over us when the mind is at its weakest.

But as the spring approaches, my spirit brightens with the lengthening of the days. Brilliant blue breaks through the clouds, and even rain is a cleansing spray that scours the rooftops and makes them glisten in the sun. The fallen leaves that clogged the gutter in winter have blown away, and young buds are shooting forth on the tree outside my window.

'I'm glad you found these rooms,' I tell Henri[[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_c_one_2: , who with typical perceptiveness had me moved from the old lodgings in the Latin Quarter to speed my recovery]].

'It promises to be a divine spring,' he says. 'Now you will speedily convalesce and we'll enjoy ourselves like old times.'

I arrange for us to have dinner with Professor Waldman. Our encounter is strange. My feelings for him have always been a mixture of affection and reverence. It's almost another spring now, full eighteen months since I became ill. I had intended to return to Geneva in the autumn, as I am quite fit enough now for the journey, but there was some difficulty obtaining permits to travel, and by the time they came through the roads had been made impassable by early snow.

The delay struck me very bitterly. I began at last to realize how long I had been absent from my loved ones. Perhaps it was homesickness, perhaps because the shorter days and the howling November wind reminded me of the events of that terrible night, but I suffered a relapse and for several weeks after the official celebration of the new year - Year Two of the Revolution, as we had better remember to call it - I could not get out of bed.

After that, surprisingly, my spirits revived and Henri and I spent the winter cheerfully. There was no carol service to celebrate Christmas, of course. A new law has been passed, outlawing priests who refuse to swear the oath of allegiance to the Revolution.

## 415
*(01_C8)*

I hear your sarcasm clearly enough. Let me count them for you. What state will my father be in, blaming himself, as he must, for William's death? And his only other hope for the Frankenstein name, myself, the refugee from his own conscience, guilty of crimes against God and Reason. Elizabeth perhaps still wishes to marry me, in accordance with my parents' wishes when she was first brought into our house. Yet she cannot know what changes have befallen me, whom she always loved as a brother. And if she finds me changed too much, would she still desire marriage from a sense of duty? I think she would, and that may be the most terrible of all my fears.

So then, I could start counting on the other hand, but there's a clutch of reasons to be going on with. Satisfied?

• Not good enough. They need you. — turn to 419
• Spend a few days here, then. — turn to 420

## 416
*(01_C9)*

Do you wonder? This countryside is the same through which I travelled to university, full of hope. Ahead are the dim outlines of my ancestral homeland. These are sights that evoke the feelings of youth, as if six years were a day, yet everything might be altered.

See, here is Lausanne already. The journey is almost over. How peaceful these ancient streets are. The rattling of the carriage wheels on cobblestones. A few old men pausing over coffee and chequers to watch me alight. The peal of church bells. Oh, do I have to go on? I would like to stay here for a few days.

• Out of the question! — turn to 419
• All right, but what good would that do? — turn to 418

A few old men pausing over coffee and chequers to watch me alight. The peal of church bells. Perhaps I'll stop for a while. I could tarry here a few days before going on to Geneva.

You're right. My father and my cousin have no respite from grief - why then should I? Whatever my own feelings, I must overcome this curious reluctance to move forward to confront my fate, and drive on at once to join them.

The road runs by the side of the lake, becoming narrower as I approach my native town. Where before they were hidden in the haze of distance, now the black sides of Jura and the bright summit of Mont Blanc are as solid and real as nursery toys.

I weep at the sight. Dear mountains! Clear streams! My own lovely lake! How do you welcome your wanderer? Your summits are clear. The sky and lake are blue and placid. Everything is at peace.

## 420
*(01_CD)*

I remain two days at Lausanne in my painful state of mind. I walk along the lake shore. The waters are placid, all around is calm. The snow-capped mountains, those palaces of nature, are not changed. All that astounds and expands the spirit, and fills us with awe, is in those cloud-piercing icy pinnacles. The weight of millions of years is up there. If there is a God, you will find him in the high unbreathable air of the Alps, my friend, not in some dusty chapel that smells of dead stone and incense.

## 421
*(01_CE)*

Thus restored, and in a better frame of mind to give succour to my loved ones, I hitch the ponies to the cart and continue the last few miles towards my home.

Yet, as I draw near, grief and fear again threaten to overcome me. I set out too late in the day. Already it's getting dark; the mountains are disappearing in the gloom. The whole panorama to the south appears a vast and dim scene of evil.

I foresee that I am destined to become the most wretched of human beings. Already, in my early twenties, my life seems drained of purpose. My only feelings are of tragic grandeur and artful decay. It seems that I drive through the empty world at the end of time.

## 446

That was my first thought. But when I reflect on the story that I have to tell... a being whom I myself formed and endued with life... a chance encounter at midnight among the precipices of an inaccessible mountain. Remember how Henri attributed every mention of the monster to my nervous fever? Knowledge of that illness would give an air of delirium to a tale already quite improbable. Of a certainty, if anyone were to tell me such a story, I would take them for mad.

Besides, the superhuman nature of the monster would elude all pursuit, even if I were so far credited as to persuade my relatives to commence it. And then of what use would be pursuit? Who could arrest a creature capable of scaling the overhanging sides of Mont Salève? By this reasoning, I am resolved to remain silent.

Oh, that fire is good. I hadn't realized how the cold had got into my bones overnight.

How strange to be back home. Six years have elapsed like a dream, but for one indelible trace, and here I stand in the same spot where I last embraced my father before setting off to university.

The room seems smaller than I remember, of course - everyone says that, but it's true all the same. And how odd to gaze on the familiar objects of childhood - that carpet with its pattern of peacocks and foliage, the birds' eggs my father collects in this case, the spines of the books like old friends. You know, it is good to be home but at the same time there is something dreadful about it. As though the child we once were had become a ghost trapped amid all these memories.

The trial begins. After the advocate against her has stated the charge, several witnesses are called. Before long, if I didn't know her for a fact to be innocent, I admit I would start to have doubts.

The facts are damning. She was out the whole of the night on which the murder was committed. Towards morning she was seen by a market-woman not far from the spot where William's body was afterwards found. The woman asked Justine what she was doing there, but she looked very strangely and only returned a confused and unintelligible answer. She returned to the house about eight o'clock in the morning, and when the cook asked where she had spent the night, she replied that she had been looking for William and demanded earnestly if there had been any news. When shown his body, she fell into violent hysterics and kept to her bed for several days.

The advocate now brings out the brooch that the servant found in Justine's pocket. He calls on Elizabeth, who testifies in a faltering voice that it was the same that, an hour before the child was missed, she had placed round his neck. At this, a murmur of horror and indignation fills the court.

## 533
*(01_FK)*

She is hanged the next day. Apart from a priest, the executioner and a few court officials, I am the only one present. Justine, blindfolded, may not even have known I came.

After feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of calamities, the dead calmness of inaction and certainty that follows acts to deprive the soul both of hope and fear. Justine is dead, she rests now, and I am alive. The blood flows freely in my veins, but a weight of despair and remorse presses on my heart which nothing can remove.

In the days that follow I am unable to sleep. I wander the streets like an evil spirit. I have committed deeds of mischief beyond description, I know that, yet my heart overflows with kindness and the love of virtue. I set out on my course with benevolent intentions, thirsting for the moment when I should put my knowledge in service to my fellow beings. Now all is blasted. Instead of that serenity of conscience which would allow me to look back upon the past with self-satisfaction, and from thence to gather promise of new hopes, I am seized by remorse and the crushing sense of guilt, which hurries me on through the darkened streets, hounded by the half-dreams that sleeplessness has rendered feverish, submerged in my own hell of intense tortures such as no language can describe.

I don't say anything, but he brings me his book anyway. '*The Agonies of Young Werther*,' I read on the cover. And inside: 'Volume One.'

'Volume Two is much the same but he dies at the end,' supplies the innkeeper helpfully.

I close the book with a snap that makes him blink in surprise. 'You have decided me. Have a lunch basket made up and my mule brought to the door.'

## 560
*(01_GD)*

I rise early, refreshed, but when I draw back the curtains it is to find the rain pouring down in torrents and thick mists hiding the mountain summits. The sight depresses me, for I had hoped the rain would hold off until after my morning walk.

I cannot spend the day cooped up at the inn with Father and Elizabeth. I bolt a hasty breakfast, telling the innkeeper to have a luncheon basket made up for me, and am on my mule before I hear them stirring.

'Nasty weather, sir,' says the innkeeper from the porch, 'but I expect you won't go far.'

'On the contrary, I intend to cross the glacier,' I tell him, kicking my mule into action before Elizabeth can rush down and reproach me for abandoning her.

I remember the effect that the view of this tremendous and ever-moving glacier produced upon my mind when I first saw it. It then filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave wings to the soul, and allowed it to soar from the obscure world to light and joy. The sight of the awful and majestic in nature has always had the effect of helping me to forget the passing cares of life. Thank heaven the rain gives me the excuse of going up there alone. The presence of another would destroy the solitary grandeur of the scene.

• Of course it would. — turn to 563

## 563
*(01_GH)*

The ascent is precipitous, but the path is cut into continual short windings, which enable one to surmount the perpendicularity of the mountain. It is a terrifically desolate scene. Everywhere you can see traces of the winter avalanche, where trees lie broken on the ground.

The path, as I ascend higher, is intersected by ravines of snow, down which stones continually roll from above. One of them is particularly dangerous, as the slightest sound - even raising your voice - risks bringing destruction upon the head of the speaker.

The pines here are not tall or luxuriant, but they are sombre and add an air of severity to the scene. Pausing after an hour's ascent, I look down on the valley. Vast mists are rising from the rivers, curling in thick wreaths around the opposite mountains, whose summits are buried in the uniform clouds. It is a melancholy vista, not helped by the sheets of rain lacing down from an iron-grey sky.

Indeed. It is nearly noon when I arrive at the top of the ascent, where there is a rock overlooking the sea of ice. A mist covers both that and the surrounding mountains, but by the time I've finished lunch a breeze has blown up, dissipating the mist so that it is safe to descend onto the glacier.

The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep. The field of ice is about three miles across but it takes me nearly two hours to cross it. The opposite mountain is a bare perpendicular rock. From this side, Montanvert is exactly opposite, and above it rises, in awful majesty, the immense bulk of Mont Blanc.

I remain in a recess of the rock, gazing on this wonderful and stupendous scene. The vast river of ice winds among the mountains, whose aerial summits loom overhead. Their icy and glittering peaks shine in the sunlight over the clouds. My heart was sorrowful before, [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_d_two_3a or you have KW_d_two_7a: as you know,]]but now swells with something like joy must feel, if I can remember joy.

Let your compassion be moved, and do not disdain me. Listen to my tale. When you have heard that, abandon or commiserate me as you judge I deserve. But hear me. The guilty, whatever their deeds, are allowed to speak in their own defence before they are condemned. You accuse me of murder and you would, with a satisfied conscience, destroy your own creature. Oh, praise the eternal justice of man! Yet I ask you not to spare me. Come with me, Frankenstein. Only listen to my story - and then, if you can and if you will, destroy the work of your hands.'

## 628
*(01_IC)*

The melancholy mood into which I sank following William's murder is gradually passing, but every now and then it surges back without warning. On those days a devouring blackness overcasts the sun. I can bear no company or even walls around me and, fleeing as it were in horror from the stifling bosom of the family, I take refuge in the most perfect solitude. I pass whole days on the lake alone in a little boat, watching the clouds, and listening to the rippling of the waves, silent and listless. The fresh air and bright sun seldom fails to restore me to some degree of composure and, on my return, I am able to tolerate the salutations of my friends with a readier smile and a more cheerful heart.

On one such occasion, when the clink of teacups over breakfast rasps my nerves and every muttered pleasantry makes me want to lash out at them, I tell my father and Elizabeth that I will be spending the day walking in the hills along the lake.

'Oh, Victor,' says Elizabeth brightly, 'do you remember how you and I and Henri used to play along the shore? We would go for miles, inventing stories in which you and Henri were buccaneers, vying to carry away your little prize. Let me come with you today!'

• Good grief, she's as tenacious as the monster. — turn to 629

She gets up and sweeps out of the room. 'For heaven's sake, Victor,' says my father, 'at least wait until you're married before you start having such pointless rows.'

I have seen that lake agitated by a tempest, when the wind tore up whirlwinds of water. I have seen the mountains of La Valais, and the Pays de Vaud. But *this* country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders. The mountains of Switzerland are more majestic and strange, but there is a charm in the banks of this divine river that I never before saw equalled. Look at the castle there that overhangs yon precipice. How did they build that? And another on that island, look, almost concealed amongst the foliage. And now that group of labourers coming from among their vines. And there's a village tucked away in the recess of the mountain. Nearly missed that. Look, Victor, look! Surely, the spirit that inhabits and guards this place has a soul more in harmony - '

'Yes. Pass that bottle before you have quite drained it.'

'This bottle? This cherished amphora, you mean, which contains the oil that fires the lamp of poetry? Bottled at the Hippocrene - '

'According to the label, it was bottled at Oberwesel.'

'Oh, you are just a scientist. Facts are all you care about. There is no hope for you.'

## 663
*(01_JC)*

Our next stop is Oxford. Unlike Paris, where the university nests within the bosom of the city, here the magnificent colleges, interwoven by the lovely silver thread of the Isis and with stone walls and spires ablaze in the cold January light, create an impression of an Empyrean realm dedicated to the sacred pursuit of knowledge.

After a few days, however, my elation is tinged with disappointment. Oxford's curriculum elevates the arts but, in the sciences, places more emphasis on the teachings of the past than on the uncovering of nature's many still-guarded secrets. Bacon taught the supreme importance of empirical methods, but these scholars of today content themselves merely with endless discussion of his experiments.

At one lecture, my patience wears so thin that, under the pretext of asking a question, I draw attention to a number of developments in biology and chemistry of which the professor seems unaware. Our dispute creates a stir of excitement among the students, who previously gave every impression of slumber. To give him credit, rather than taking offence, he encourages me to speak and afterwards approaches me with an invitation to dine at his college.

## 664
*(01_JD)*

We have a glass of sherry in the common room and then, to my astonishment, one of the dons opens the window, swings his legs over the sill and disappears from view. Others follow and I experience a momentary dreamlike dislocation of reality as I imagine them all jumping to their deaths in the night. Then my host explains, 'It's the quickest way to reach the hall. Across the roof, you see.'

I follow him. Outside, the flat roof is awash with rain and the dons hurry, hunched over, towards the door of the dining hall. In their slick black robes they look like great hopping crows.

My host and I have just been discussing the effect of ethyl mesylate on living cells. Shouting the last part of what I was saying, I brace myself for a dash through the pelting rain when he catches my arm. I recognize the look. What a time to be struck by a profound thought - but, I appreciate, we must respect the moment, for inspiration is not in our control. Therefore we stand together, soaking up water like two strips of blotting paper, discussing Man's progress at prising out the pearls God left hidden. And all the while the lightning crashes overhead.

'Oh my, we're getting quite wet,' he says after a while. 'And instead of feeding you, here I am picking your brains.'

'I only hope my theories have some practical application in your own work, Professor Tyrell.'

According to his own account, he was attacked and robbed. The first I know of it is when I am awoken by someone stumbling about in the parlour that adjoins our two bedrooms. I emerge bleary-eyed to find Henri wilted in a chair, a blood-soaked rag pressed to his bruised and lacerated face.

'Let me do that, I'm a doctor.'

'Not actually a doctor yet,' he mumbles through swollen lips.

'Well, if you were dead I could cut you up competently enough. This water is no good, it needs to be hot. I'll ring for the maid.'

He is quite a mess. Apart from the blood, his jacket is covered in muddy boot-prints. 'I am thinking of a career as a welcome mat,' he says. Then, 'Ow!' as laughter splits his lip again.

'What happened?'

He waves it away. 'I took an injudicious short cut by the docks.'

I cannot imagine which two clubs or dinner parties might have adjoined that part of town, but I have noticed that Henri has a taste for some rough dives. I don't press him on it.

## 672
*(01_JL)*

In a coffee house near the university, I encounter the celebrated Dr Robert Campbell. To the dismay of the waiters, we are soon sketching out our theories with the aid of napkins.

'You must work on your surgical techniques,' Campbell tells me. 'A man who is only speculative in anatomy and does not learn to be both practical and accurate is doomed to remain a dabbler.'

'Are there any lectures you can recommend?'

'Lectures? You're not listening to me, Frankenstein. You need to grab a knife - well, this is a spoon, but it will do to illustrate. Put your hand to it. Learn to dissect every part. Each bit of the body is an ingenious machine. You Swiss like your clocks, I'm told. And do you go to lectures to learn about clocks? No, you *take them apart.*'

'Shall I help you with that cake, sir?' ventures a waiter.

Campbell waves him away and mangles a couple of slices for us using the spoon. 'Correct tools help also,' he says with a smile. 'Get yourself some good surgical instruments from Nicolson in Drummond Street, and come along to my classes at the Company of Surgeons.'

'I must, with regret, decline your offer,' I tell Campbell. 'I have a certain project that demands my full attention, and it would be a waste to attend your classes without being able to devote myself to them.'

He gives me such a penetrating look that for a shocking moment I feel as if he has peeled away my every defence and can see the secrets of my innermost heart.

He produces a loud belch. 'That's better. Too much sugar and tea sloshing around in the guts can play the very devil with digestion. Now, what were we saying? Oh, you can't see your way to it, then? That's too bad. You're a bright fellow, Frankenstein, but I have a feeling you're one of those that wants to run before you can walk.'

We say our affable farewells and I go back to the lodgings to prepare for the next and final stage of my journey.

Under Campbell's tutelage, I am soon accomplished with the scalpel and have a thorough understanding of the workings of the human body. Unlike the surgical lectures at the university, his private classes are not just demonstrations in a theatre. We students are expected to get our hands thoroughly dirty, and thanks to a steady supply of cadavers I do so.

Each day - no, each minute of his instruction reveals to me the mistakes and oversights I made when constructing the original monster. Now I can work on a more delicate scale.

'I never thought, as a student of the sciences, that I would need to become an artist too,' I say to him one day as we're washing our hands.

'Man, if you had said that to Leonardo or Michelangelo!' he scoffs. 'They'd have thought you stark mad.'

## 689
*(01_JY · Trust thread 0)*

One of the remotest of the islands. It's perfect for my purposes, being hardly more than a rock whose high sides are continually beaten by the waves. The soil is barren, scarcely affording a living for its half-dozen gaunt inhabitants. Food and even fresh water must be procured from the mainland some five miles away.

There are just three miserable huts on the whole island. The one I have hired comprises two rooms, and would be better described as a stable than a house. The thatch has fallen in, the walls are unplastered, and the door is off its hinges.

'You'll no doubt want it done up a wee bit,' says the man who is renting it to me, using the same tone with which an undertaker offers the bereaved a choice of coffins.

I order only the most essential repairs. When my few sticks of furniture arrive from the mainland, the hovel is almost habitable. I feared my arrival might stir up gossip, but the senses of the cottagers here have been benumbed by want and squalid poverty. So I am left entirely alone on the headland.

• Alone but for the monster, perhaps. — turn to 691

## 711
*(01_K9 · Trust thread 0)*

[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize:

What's that? There, at the window - it is the monster! So it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize:

What's that? There, at the window - it is he! So he]] did indeed follow me, marking every step of my progress, and now is here to claim the fulfilment of my promise.

How powerfully our memories can be stimulated by the senses. As I close the circuit, there comes the familiar snap of electrical force, the acrid tang in the air, the acid flavour on the tongue and the faint odour of singed hair. With this instantaneous barrage of impressions, that come more swiftly than I am able to describe them, the intervening three years are dissolved away and I feel myself transported back to that rain-lashed garret in Paris.

As then, a moment of heart-stopping silence is followed by the twitch of new muscles stirring to life. Her eyes open - the pupils of equal dimensions, adjusting satisfactorily to the dim lamplight. Her pulse is strong, settling down to the forty beats per minute that I recorded in the original experiment three years ago.
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom:

Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom:

The monster]] is beside me. We watch, both silent and awestruck, as the second of [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his]] race rises and takes her first steps. And there - hear the sound of her breath! That life *didn't exist* minutes ago. I did this. I, Frankenstein, created woman!

## 721
*(01_KE · Trust thread 0)*

I thought that would intrigue you. I had the idea back in Paris, after seeing a veteran hurrying up the street on a wooden peg leg, and I realized it is not necessary to use pre-existing body parts for the entire skeleton. My first thought was to have the long bones carved in hardwood, and then bone grafts would only be needed where the ligaments are anchored. But those would not be capable of regeneration, and my desire was to make a living creature, not a mechanical automaton. So then I remembered 'of his bones are coral made'. A good strong substance, coral. I could reverse Alonso's fate and make my creature's bones from it.

The inspiration came too late for me to incorporate it into [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom's]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the original monster's]] design, but this is one of many improvements. See this femur. Indistinguishable from a human bone, apart from the pinkish hue, but it is twice as strong - and lighter, feel. Now I must put it back into the chemical bath. None of these components are stable until connected together and energized.

## 733
*(01_KK · Trust thread 0)*

> Note the keyword KW_beautiful.

She takes shape under my hands and she is lovely. More perfect than any woman can be who is formed by the grossness of life and worn, no matter how subtly, by the rough treatment of daily existence. My creature, my Pandora, by contrast is as radiant and flawless as an angel that has found embodiment on Earth. Her very flesh, cultured without blemish, proportioned to Classical standards, glows like the full moon. The ritual of continually adjusting the flow of chemicals that nurture her perfection, the act of shaping her limbs and running my fingers across her skin - in doing these things, I feel almost as if I am performing some new kind of sacrament.

These days it is all too easy to get lost in my work. Sometimes I am surprised by the dawn, having lost hours in unconscious contemplation of my creation. Now she is almost complete. I am just draining the tank, transferring her slender form to the trestle on which I will apply the vitalizing charge, when I become aware that the sun is setting. Reaching for the lantern, my gaze strays up to the window and with a start I see [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the demon]][[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: there. An obscene grin is stamped upon its bony red face.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: there. An obscene grin is stamped upon his bony red face.]]

## 743
*(01_KP · Trust thread 0)*

As I proceed in my labour, it becomes ever more horrible and irksome to me. Sometimes I cannot prevail on myself to enter my workshop for several days. At other times I toil through the night in order to hasten completion of the filthy thing. It is a truly vile process. During my first experiment, a kind of enthusiastic frenzy blinded me to the horror of what I was doing. My mind was intently fixed on the final goal, and my eyes were shut to the horror of my proceedings. But this time I went into it in cold blood, and my heart often sickens at the work of my hands. Employed in this most detestable occupation, and immersed in a solitude where nothing ever calls my attention from the actual scene in which I am engaged, I daily grow more restless and nervous.

• It will soon be finished. — turn to 747

## 753
*(01_KU · Trust thread 0)*

How powerfully our memories can be stimulated by the senses. As I close the circuit, there comes the familiar snap of electrical force, the acrid tang in the air, the acid flavour on the tongue and the faint odour of singed hair. With this instantaneous barrage of impressions, that come more swiftly than I am able to describe them, the intervening three years are dissolved away and I feel myself transported back to that rain-lashed garret in Paris.

As then, a moment of heart-stopping silence is followed by the twitch of new muscles stirring to life. Her eyes open - the pupils of equal dimensions, adjusting satisfactorily to the dim lamplight. Her pulse is strong, settling down to the forty beats per minute that I recorded in the original experiment three years ago.
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom:

Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom:

The monster]] is beside me. We watch, both silent and awestruck, as the second of [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his]] race rises and takes her first steps. And there - hear the sound of her breath! That life *didn't exist* minutes ago. I did this. I, Frankenstein, created woman!

Suddenly she's silent. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: The creature]] and I stand frozen. For my part, I am chilled - not so much by the unearthly sound she made, as by the horrible understanding that drew it from her. It takes me a moment too long to react as I see her hand go to the bench beside her.

The scalpel catches a splinter of dazzling light from the lantern, only to be instantly dimmed by the swift flow of synthesized blood. She falls, pulling the bench down on top of her with a crash of chemical instruments, as the pool of blood spreads rapidly across the floor. The scalpel drops from her twitching fingers, her yellow eyes glaze over, and I don't need to feel for a pulse.

• She's dead. — turn to 770

## 797
*(01_L9 · Trust thread -1)*

My bedroom is dark, but I don't feel like lighting a lamp. Outside the window the sea lies motionless, with hardly a breath of wind to disturb the dead silence. The moon shines down from a cloudless indigo sky. I feel like the only living thing in creation.

Hours pass. There is the creak of hinges as the outer door is slowly opened. All at once I'm trembling. I want to call out - there's a cottage not far from mine, and if they hear me they will come to help. But my throat is paralyzed. It's like one of those nightmares when you try in vain to run, to cry out, but you are held helpless by fright.

• Then you can only wait to confront your monster. — turn to 801

## 817
*(01_LE · Trust thread -1)*

'I was weak,' I say. 'I admit it. But no longer. You have no power over me now. All your threats can achieve is to strengthen my resolve not to create you a companion with whom to procreate your wicked breed across the globe. Shall I, in cold blood, set loose upon the Earth a demon, whose delight is in death and cruelty? Get out. If you say another word you will only exasperate my rage, and then beware in case I uncreate what I have created.'

The monster reads the determination in my face, and gnashes [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his]] teeth in impotent anger. 'Shall each man find a wife for his bosom, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone? I had feelings of affection, and they were repaid with detestation and scorn. Man, you may hate - but you beware. Your hours will pass in dread and misery, and soon the bolt will fall which will destroy your happiness forever. Are you to be happy while I grovel in the intensity of my wretchedness? You can blast my other passions, but revenge remains - revenge, henceforth dearer to me than warmth or food! I may die - perhaps you know a way to destroy me - but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery. Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom. Man, you shall repent of the injuries you inflict.'

Shall I, in cold blood, set loose upon the Earth a demon, whose delight is in death and cruelty? Get out. If you say another word you will only exasperate my rage, and then beware in case I uncreate what I have created.'

The monster reads the determination in my face, and gnashes [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his]] teeth in impotent anger. 'Shall each man find a wife for his bosom, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone? I had feelings of affection, and they were repaid with detestation and scorn. Man, you may hate - but you beware. Your hours will pass in dread and misery, and soon the bolt will fall which will destroy your happiness forever. Are you to be happy while I grovel in the intensity of my wretchedness? You can blast my other passions, but revenge remains - revenge, henceforth dearer to me than warmth or food! I may die - perhaps you know a way to destroy me - but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery. Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom. Man, you shall repent of the injuries you inflict.'

# PART FIVE — 'I WILL BE WITH YOU ON YOUR WEDDING NIGHT'

## 860
*(01_LP · Trust thread -2)*

[ILLUSTRATION: pic5_1.jpg]

*May my fears,
My filial fears, be vain! and may the vaunts
And menace of the vengeful enemy
Pass like the gust, that roared and died away
In the distant tree: which heard, and only heard
In this low dell, bowed not the delicate grass.*

**CHAPTER ONE**
*The Moment of Darkness*

I walk about the island, a restless spectre. At noon, with the sun beating down strongly despite the chill wind off the sea, I am abruptly overcome by fatigue. Stretching out on the grass, I soon fall into a deep sleep, which restores me, and on awakening towards sunset I feel again as if I belong to a race of human beings like myself.

Now I am able to reflect with greater composure on what has passed, but still [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the fiend]]'s words ring in my ears like a death-knell. *I will be with you on your wedding night.* Already it is a phrase that has taken on the character of a pronouncement in one of Perrault's fairy tales, doomy and yet dreamlike, with a dream's ability to be both more and less tangible than life.

A fishing boat arrives with a packet of letters for me. There is one from Elizabeth and one from Henri.

• Read Elizabeth's. — turn to 865
• Read Henri's. — turn to 870
• They will keep. You have things you must do first. — turn to 875

## 895
*(01_LX · Trust thread -2)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

Not quite yet. I must wait for the moon to come up. At about two in the morning I cast off. There are a few other boats on the water but I steer well clear of them. At a point some four miles out, feeling as if I am carrying out a dreadful crime, I heave the basket over the side. At first, despite the weight of stones, it only bobs on the waves and I feel growing panic. Then bubbles start to stream up around it and with a gurgling sound it sinks from view. I breathe again.

As I sail on, the sky begins to cloud over. A strengthening breeze blows from the northeast and the sea becomes choppy. We could be in for quite a storm.

• Sail on. — turn to 901
• Turn back. — turn to 906

## 911
*(01_M0 · Trust thread -3)*

Nonsense. I'm an excellent sailor - I've been going out on the lake at home since I was eight years old. I am surprised and disappointed that after all this time you so little know me that you think I would timidly flee back to dry land at the first gust of wind. In fact the breeze is quite refreshing. I shall set the tiller and sit back a while, luxuriating in this all too brief period when, under the timeless roof of the stars, I can forget the cares that freight my life.

• If you say so. — turn to 900

## 916
*(01_M1 · Trust thread -3)*

I am a good sailor but I don't know these waters, so perhaps you're right. Turning about, I return to the island and wait to go back with the next packet boat. The skipper is an old fisherman whose face is so leathery and lined that I would reject it as a component for building one of my creations.

'Bit different from the wee ponds ye'd be used to back home, no doubt,' are the only words he speaks to me on the entire voyage, this statement being accompanied by a laconic nod that seems to imply ownership of the entire Pentland Firth.

Arriving in Perth, I head to the lodging house where Henri and I arranged to meet. I hope I haven't kept him waiting. With my grisly task behind me, my thoughts are filled with plans for where we should travel next.

The manager gives me a cheerful greeting, but his manner becomes uncomfortable when I sign my name in his book. He hands me a note that requests me to call on a Mr Kirkdale, at an address in the town.

'And who is Mr Kirkdale?'

'He's a magistrate.'

He pretends to find something of importance in his ledgers. He is being very evasive.

• Demand that he tells you what's going on. — turn to 949
• Go and see this man Kirkdale. — turn to 957

'Bit different from the wee ponds ye'd be used to back home, no doubt,' are the only words he speaks to me on the entire voyage, this statement being accompanied by a laconic nod that seems to imply ownership of the entire Pentland Firth.

Arriving in Perth, I head to the lodging house where Henri and I arranged to meet. I hope I haven't kept him waiting. With my grisly task behind me, my thoughts are filled with plans for where we should travel next.

The manager gives me a cheerful greeting, but his manner becomes uncomfortable when I sign my name in his book. He hands me a note that requests me to call on a Mr Kirkdale, at an address in the town.

'And who is Mr Kirkdale?'

'He's a magistrate.'

He pretends to find something of importance in his ledgers. He is being very evasive.

• Demand that he tells you what's going on. — turn to 953
• Go and see this man Kirkdale. — turn to 961

## 921
*(01_M2 · Trust thread -3)*

Immeasurable grey leagues stretch all around me, the waters roaring and buffeting my little vessel. I brought no compass, and am so little acquainted with the geography of this part of the world that the sun is of little use.

How long did I sleep? Perhaps twelve hours - I was still exhausted from my sleepless night when [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the monster]] came. Given the strength of the wind, and if it hasn't changed direction in all that time, I could be a hundred miles out into the Atlantic. Already I feel the torment of a burning thirst, a prelude to my other sufferings.

I look to the heavens, which are covered by clouds that fly before the wind only to be replaced by others. I look upon the sea and wonder if it is to be my grave. 'Fiend,' I exclaim, 'your task is already fulfilled!' I think of Elizabeth, of my father, and of Henri, and sink back in the boat. Helplessness has robbed me of my strength. My only companions are fear and despair.

## 933
*(01_M5 · Trust thread -3)*

Hours pass. By degrees, as the sun dips towards the horizon, the wind drops to a gentle breeze and the sea becomes free from breakers. But these give place to a heavy swell. Feeling sick, I am hardly able to hold the rudder when suddenly I see a line of high land towards the south. And so I arrive safely on the coast of Scotland.

Arriving in Perth, I head to the lodging house where Henri and I arranged to meet. I hope I haven't kept him waiting. With my grisly task behind me, my thoughts are filled with plans for where we should travel next.

The manager gives me a cheerful greeting, but his manner becomes uncomfortable when I sign my name in his book. He hands me a note that requests me to call on a Mr Kirkdale, at an address in the town.

'And who is Mr Kirkdale?'

'He's a magistrate.'

He pretends to find something of importance in his ledgers. He is being very evasive.

• Demand that he tells you what's going on. — turn to 949
• Go and see this man Kirkdale. — turn to 957

## 941
*(01_M6 · Trust thread -3)*

Hours pass. By degrees, as the sun dips towards the horizon, the wind drops to a gentle breeze and the sea becomes free from breakers. But these give place to a heavy swell. Feeling sick, I am hardly able to hold the rudder when suddenly I see a line of high land towards the south. After the fatigue and dreadful suspense of the last few hours, this sudden certainty of life rushes like a flood of warm joy to my heart, and my view of the approaching coastline is blurred by tears

How mutable are our feelings, and how strange is that clinging love we have of life even in the excess of misery. The sail is torn, but I contrive another with my cloak. The shore has a wild and rocky appearance but is obviously more populated than the barren isle I left. There are vessels near the shore, and find myself suddenly transported back to the neighbourhood of civilised man.

I follow the coast and soon the steeple of a church appears from behind a small promontory. It stands in a neat town of whitewashed houses. Exhausted and thirsty, I sail directly into the harbour, my heart bounding with joy at my unexpected escape.

Several fishermen saunter over as I am fixing the boat and arranging the sails. Hearing them speak English, I ask them in that language where I have been swept to.

'He wants to know the name of this place, is that it?' says one old man.

'It's Carrick,' says a younger man.

'In Scotland?'

He laughs. 'Some navigators you foreigners are. It's Ireland, man.'

• Find a place to stay. — turn to 1023
• Better unload your chemical apparatus first. — turn to 999
