The shore has a wild and rocky appearance but is obviously more populated than the barren isle I left. There are vessels near the shore, and find myself suddenly transported back to the neighbourhood of civilised man.

I follow the coast and soon the steeple of a church appears from behind a small promontory. It stands in a neat town of whitewashed houses. Exhausted and thirsty, I sail directly into the harbour, my heart bounding with joy at my unexpected escape.

Several fishermen saunter over as I am fixing the boat and arranging the sails. Hearing them speak English, I ask them in that language where I have been swept to.

'He wants to know the name of this place, is that it?' says one old man.

'It's Carrick,' says a younger man.

'In Scotland?'

He laughs. 'Some navigators you foreigners are. It's Ireland, man.'

I find myself outside Kirkdale's house, the note with his address in my hand. I feel like a sleepwalker, hardly aware of how I got here. After a few minutes in a gloomy dark-panelled study, I hear the door open and look up into the face of an kindly looking man.

'I am Monsieur Clerval's friend,' I tell him, though he must know that already. 'I'd like to know how he died.'

He tells you that Henri was found on the mud by the river at low tide, just two days ago.

'We were supposed to meet here,' I say. 'We are on a tour of the British Isles.'

'Yes, so he mentioned to the owner of your lodging house.'

'How did he die? Did he drown?'

'Drown?' Kirkdale removes his glasses and breathes on the lenses before polishing them. 'He hadn't fallen into the river, Mr Frankenstein. I'm sorry, I thought you'd been told. He was beaten to death.'

'Where is the body?'

'You don't need to identify him. We have his possessions and the manager's statement for that. I say this because - well, never a pretty sight, a dead body, but it may not be the image you'd like to remember.'

> If Empathy > 1: Note the keyword KW_split_to_18a.
> If Empathy ≤ 1 and Empathy > -2: Note the keyword KW_split_to_18.
> If Empathy ≤ 1 and Empathy ≤ -2: Note the keyword KW_split_to_17b.

[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 1:

I enter the room where Henri's coffin lies. How can I describe my sensations? I am parched with horror. Kirkdale seems to become like smoke, blown away. The room is darkness. There is nothing else in creation except for me and the broken, lifeless form of Henri Clerval, my lifelong friend. I reach out to touch his hand and, feeling the terrible coldness where there will never be warmth again, I give an anguished cry. 'My dearest friend, I did this to you!'

Kirkdale tries to lead me away. Perhaps pull me away. His voice is saying I mustn't blame myself, mustn't blame myself.

'Then who should I blame? God? The devil? He is my third victim. How Death must laugh - I set out to conquer him, but all I have done is consign three people to his care! And there will be more!'

I'm not sure what happens next. I think I try to embrace the corpse. There is shouting. Men burst into the room and drag me away from poor Henri's side. Someone says, 'He's lost his wits!'

I suppose my nerves simply spool out beyond their endurance. The darkness at the edge of my vision grows to swallow me and then I vanish too, mere smoke like Kirkdale and the others, and there is nothing at all left except for the baleful, invisible, but palpable presence of the monster.]]
[[If Empathy ≤ 1, read the following:]]

I enter the room where Henri's coffin lies. How can I describe my sensations on beholding his face? It is as though, far away, there is a tumult of great anguish but I am in the eye of the storm and can hear and feel nothing.

The undertaker has worked his art skilfully, but there is no disguising the tracery of lacerations under a heavy caking of powder. I lean forward. Kirkdale puts his hand on my arm.

'I am a doctor,' I tell him.

'Even so, sir, please.'

I have seen enough to know that my friend was bludgeoned to death. A very horrible and sustained attack that must have gone on long after he lost consciousness.

'We think several men... They may have been disturbed while trying to dispose of the body, as no money was taken.' As we leave the room, he says, 'Do you have any idea who killed your friend, Mr Frankenstein?'
[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 1 and Empathy > -2:

'Oh yes,' I say calmly. 'I did.']][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ -2:

'None at all.']]

→ If Empathy > 1 and (Empathy > 1 or Empathy ≤ -2), turn to 1131.
→ If Empathy ≤ 1 and Empathy > -2, turn to 1131.

• [If Empathy ≤ -2] 'What is being done to find the killer?' — turn to 990
• [If Empathy ≤ -2] Go back to your lodgings. — turn to 973

'We think he was killed by more than one man,' says Kirkdale.

'What makes you say that?'

'The extent of his injuries.' He spreads his hands, doesn't want to talk about it. 'Are you all right, Mr Frankenstein?'

'The shock... I think I'd better go and lie down.'

'Of course.'

He shows me to the door. My pulse is racing and the hall seems to press in on me, hot and heavy. I pull away from his handshake and hurry out into the fresh air, desperate to get away. Except that, from the thing that pursues me, I know there is no escape.

**END OF CHAPTER ONE**

## 999
*(01_ME · Trust thread -3)*

'Give you a hand?' offers a young man with a smiling, freckled face.

'Thank you.' I gather my clothes and notebooks, and as he jumps down into the boat I nod towards the tarpaulin in the bow. 'There are some boxes there I'll need delivered to my lodgings.'

I'm getting out of the boat when I sense a sudden tension in the crowd. They're staring past me. I turn and see the young man, his freckles now standing out on a very pale face, hastily lowering the tarpaulin.

'What is it?' I say.

He gives me a stricken look, then seems to recover his wits. 'Grab him!' he says. And several onlookers step forward to seize my arms.

• Ask what is under the tarpaulin. — turn to 1015

*(01_ME · Trust thread -1)*

'Give you a hand?' offers a young man with a smiling, freckled face.

'Thank you.' I gather my clothes and notebooks, and as he jumps down into the boat I nod towards the tarpaulin in the bow. 'There are some boxes there I'll need delivered to my lodgings.'

I'm getting out of the boat when I sense a sudden tension in the crowd. They're staring past me. I turn and see the young man, his freckles now standing out on a very pale face, hastily lowering the tarpaulin.

'What is it?' I say.

He gives me a stricken look, then seems to recover his wits. 'Grab him!' he says. And several onlookers step forward to seize my arms.

*(01_MH · Trust thread -3)*

I take lodgings at an inn near the wharf and spend the afternoon planning my itinerary to rendezvous with Henri in Perth. The town of Carrick, though pleasant enough, is rather isolated, so getting by carriage to Belfast is likely to take longer than the sea voyage around the coast of Scotland. I could take my sloop, of course, but the storm has quashed my enthusiasm for sailing.

That reminds me, I had better fetch my equipment. I am on the point of ringing a bell to get some servants from the inn to help me, but there will be plenty of willing workers down at the quayside.

'What is the meaning of this? Innkeeper, fetch the police.'

'They are the polis, sir.' He turns to the roughest-looking of the men. 'What are you about, McCluskey? Manhandling this gentleman?'

## 1055
*(01_ML · Trust thread -3)*

> Note the keyword KW_split_to_26.

Hearing my cries for help, a crowd soon gathers. Steeling myself, I draw back the tarpaulin. The body is lying face down, but even as I reach to turn it over, I know. The dead face that is revealed to me is that of my dearest friend.

'Henri!'

'Do you know this man?' says a rough-looking fellow with an air of authority.

I slump in the bottom of the boat, holding poor Henri's cold white hand. The marks of the monster's fingers are still on his neck.

'I do,' I manage to sob out as tears stream down my cheeks.

'Then you'd better come with us.'

Still weeping uncontrollably, I am dragged in front of the local magistrate, a man called Kirwan. Numbly I give my name and a muddled account of how I come to be here.

'And can you explain how Mr Clerval met his demise, Mr Frankenstein.'

I don't care anymore. With Henri's death, surely [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom has attained]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the demon has attained]][[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: his]] acme of spite against me.

'I killed him,' I reply.

And at that the darkness closes in, the room spirals into a blur around me, and I fall gratefully into the arms of oblivion.

→ Turn to 1131.

## 1063
*(01_MM · Trust thread -3)*

Steeling myself, I draw back the tarpaulin. The body is lying face down, but even as I reach to turn it over, I know. The dead face that is revealed to me is Henri's.

I fall back in the bottom of the boat, having to grit my teeth to stifle a howl of anguish that would bring half the town running. Somehow I keep enough presence of mind to throw the tarpaulin back over the body before anybody should see him. The sight of those staring eyes remains imprinted on my vision. It seem as if I will carry it to my dying day.
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom:

Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom:

The monster]] must have murdered him, anticipating a calamitous outcome to the recent experiments, and left his body here to draw the blame onto my head. Cursed fiend! Exquisitely cruel demon! To devise a strategy that has, in one stroke, robbed me of my dearest friend and nearly put my head in the noose for it.

• Find a magistrate and explain what happened. — turn to 1071
• No one has seen him. Dispose of the body. — turn to 1079

## 1076
*(01_MN · Trust thread 2)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

> Note the keyword KW_split_to_26.

Mr Kirwan, the local magistrate, seems a benevolent and mild-mannered old man, but his compassionate smile turns steadily to a frown as I set out my story.

'Well now, it's an extraordinary tale, Mr Frankenstein.'

He doesn't believe me. I am too sick at heart to defend myself. 'In truth, I am his murderer,' I say, trembling uncontrollably. 'I am to blame for my brother's death, too - for which another hanged, an innocent. The world would be better off without me.'

'Now I have two stories!' says Kirwan, his patience wearing thin. 'There is another murderer at large, or you committed the crime yourself?'

I lift my gaze to his. All light has gone out of the world. What does anything matter now? The room, the old man, the crackling fire in the hearth, the darkening sky outside - they blur and spin around me, and I know no more.

→ Turn to 1136.

## 1122
*(01_MU · Trust thread -4)*

> Note the keyword KW_split_to_26.

I am brought to the room where the corpse lies. How can I describe my sensations? I am parched with horror. The magistrate and witnesses seem to step back out of the physical space around the coffin. I and the lifeless form of Henri Clerval are the only players on the stage.

With a dreamlike dislocation, I observe my own reactions - just as, I am aware, Kirwan is observing them. Seizing the cold hand, I give an anguished cry full of guilt and regret. 'My dearest friend, I did this to you!'

Kirwan steps from the wings. I hardly notice him, so intent am I on the blank clay that used to contain the vital spirit of my friend.

'Are you confessing to this man's murder, Frankenstein?'

'Not him alone. I have a string of victims. He's the third. How Death must laugh - I set out to conquer him, but all I have done is consign three people to his care! And there will be more!'

I'm not sure what happens next. I think I try to embrace the corpse. There is shouting. Hands drag me away. Someone says, 'He's mad!' Another: 'Stop him!'

Whether a blow is struck or my nerves simply spool out beyond their endurance, I cannot say. But the darkness at the edge of my vision grows to swallow me and then there is no one on the stage but for the baleful, invisible, but palpable presence of the monster.

**END OF CHAPTER ONE**

• CHAPTER TWO — turn to 1139

Kirkdale sends a note about Henri's funeral. I mean to go but am still in bed at the time the service is due to begin.
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize:

It]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize:

He]] has crushed me,' I write to my father. 'Be on your guard, for a doom follows everyone I love.'

## 1158
*(01_MY · Trust thread -4 to -3)*

I talk at length, but he isn't really listening. 'Mr Frankenstein,' he says, 'I would advise you to put all this speculation out of your head. There isn't any need to go looking for complex motives and ravening fiends and what-have-you. I'm sorry to say it, but a man who chooses Mr Clerval's way of life is going to mix with certain elements - '

'What do you mean by these insinuations? I tell you, he was killed by a creature [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: that]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: who]] has sworn to make me suffer.'

'Are you familiar with Occam's razor, Mr Frankenstein?'

'I am a scientist. So of course I am.'

'Well, we're scientists in our way too. And I can tell you that there's nothing in Mr Clerval's sad case that impels the law to extend its enquiries.' Kirkdale gets his hat and cane. At the door, he turns. 'If you'll forgive me saying so, I think you should see a physician. You may not be aware how much this affair has taken its toll on you.'

• He's right. — turn to 1167
• Ask him about Henri's funeral. — turn to 1184

After a few days, having belatedly accepted that I am in no state to travel alone, I am pleased to receive a note from my father saying that he is on his way. We will travel home together.

The weeks pass slowly, the summer a turmoil of overwhelming clouds, oppressively close days, and crashing thunderstorms - or so it seems to me, for whom the sun has been forever darkened by Henri's death. Alone in a strange place, I start at every step on the path outside at night, and I both dread and hope for the heavy tread on the stairs that would end my despair.

At last, in the middle of a sweltering afternoon in which the whole city lies drugged like a patient awaiting an operation, a carriage stops in front of my lodgings. Down in the street, a familiar figure raises his hand. I smile for the first time since my interview with the magistrate, and hurry down to greet my father.

'Victor,' he says, trying to hide the concern he must feel at seeing me so drawn and pale, 'it is so good to see you, son. Terrible what happened to Clerval. A tragic accident.'

• Agree. — turn to 1688
• Dispute that it was an accident. — turn to 1679

At last, in the middle of a sweltering afternoon in which the whole city lies drugged like a patient awaiting an operation, a carriage stops in front of my lodgings. Down in the street, a familiar figure raises his hand. I smile for the first time since my interview with the magistrate, and hurry down to greet my father.

'Victor,' he says, trying to hide the concern he must feel at seeing me so drawn and pale, 'it is so good to see you, son. Terrible what happened to Clerval. A tragic accident.'

• Agree. — turn to 1685
• Dispute that it was an accident. — turn to 1676

## 1184
*(01_N1 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'He was laid to rest in the Greyfriars cemetery in the middle of town here. It has recently been extended, so I was quite fortunate in securing a plot for him there.'

'You're very kind. I will of course pay all the bills.'

'Not a Catholic, I suppose, being Swiss?'

'Now that he's dead, it hardly matters, does it?'

'Berkeley would say that he is still an idea in the mind of God,' Kirkdale says, fetching his hat and cane. 'As are we all.'

I think it better to make no reply, so I simply wish him good day.

→ Turn to 1176.

## 1192
*(01_N2 · Trust thread -4 to -3)*

The magistrate has to investigate my claims, of course, but despite strong protestations on my part that I am responsible for Henri's death, he soon comes to other conclusions.

'Your friend frequently ventured into the, ah, let's say the seedier parts of the city,' he tells me. 'We have plenty of witnesses who can testify to that.'

We are sitting facing each other in two comfortable armchairs by a fire in a small room in his house. If not for the bars on the windows I could be a guest.

'We are not natives of this country,' I remind him. 'Henri wouldn't necessarily have realized he was straying into danger. The streets of Geneva are perfectly safe at night.'

'Come now, Mr Frankenstein, I believe your friend was a man of the world. He lived with you in Paris, did he not? And during the Reign of Terror, as it is now being called. How safe was that?'

'What of it, in any case? The murderer was watching him. When the opportunity came, [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he]] struck.'

'When you put it in those terms, it hardly seems you can claim to be describing yourself.'

• Tell him about the monster. — turn to 1211
• Admit you weren't in the city the time. — turn to 1219

## 1201
*(01_N3 · Trust thread -4)*

For a long time I writhe in a fever, only dimly aware of my surroundings. My lucid moments are few, like a drowning man surfacing and gulping at the air before the water again closes over him. I lie stretched on a bed, wound in perspiration-drenched sheets, surrounded by the quiet bustling of nurses, whispered voices, bitter medicines washed down with water trickled over my parched and unresisting lips. And the endless flicker as day follows night follows day.

Why do I not die? Death snatches away many children, the only hopes of their doting parents. How many brides and youthful lovers have been one day in the bloom of health and hope, and the next a prey for worms and the decay of the tomb? Of what materials am I made, that I can thus resist so many shocks?

But I am doomed to live. And at last my mind awakes to understanding. Morning light blazes in through the window. At first I remember only the sense of a great misfortune having overwhelmed me. Then the memories fall back into place like pieces in a jigsaw, and I give a deep groan.

A maid who is clearing my bedside table looks around with a start. 'Oh sir, you're awake.'

• Speak to her. — turn to 1498
• Ask to see Mr Kirkdale. — turn to 1528

For a long time I writhe in a fever, only dimly aware of my surroundings. My lucid moments are few, like a drowning man surfacing and gulping at the air before the water again closes over him. I lie stretched on a bed, wound in perspiration-drenched sheets, surrounded by the quiet bustling of nurses, whispered voices, bitter medicines washed down with water trickled over my parched and unresisting lips. And the endless flicker as day follows night follows day.

Why do I not die? Death snatches away many children, the only hopes of their doting parents. How many brides and youthful lovers have been one day in the bloom of health and hope, and the next a prey for worms and the decay of the tomb? Of what materials am I made, that I can thus resist so many shocks?

But I am doomed to live. And at last my mind awakes to understanding. Morning light blazes in through the window. At first I remember only the sense of a great misfortune having overwhelmed me. Then the memories fall back into place like pieces in a jigsaw, and I give a deep groan.

A maid who is clearing my bedside table looks around with a start. 'Oh sir, you're awake.'

• Speak to her. — turn to 1507
• Ask to see Mr Kirkdale. — turn to 1537

## 1211
*(01_N4 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize:

'The murderer didn't care about Henri. It wanted to strike at me by killing my dearest friend.'

'Why do you keep referring to the murderer like that? *It*, you say. Not *he*.'

'Because it is not a human being. I created it to be a man, a new kind of man, but it has forfeited its right to be considered such.'

'You created your friend's killer? You're speaking figuratively, perhaps. Some confusion between our native tongues?

'I am fluent in English, I assure you. I created the monster as a carpenter creates a cabinet.']]
[[If you do not have KW_demonize, read the following:]]

'The murderer didn't care about Henri. He wanted to strike at me by killing my dearest friend.'

'For what motive? Jealousy?'

'Jealousy, yes. He is jealous of the human race, jealous of the shrinking island of happiness which he is eroding from under me.'

'What is his name, this passionate killer?'

[[If you do not have KW_demonize and you have KW_adom, read the following:]]

'Adom. The first of his kind, you see.'

[[If you do not have KW_demonize and you do not have KW_adom, read the following:]]

'He has no name.'
[[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize:

'And where does he live?'

'In my shadow.']]

Kirkdale looks at me thoughtfully. 'I am concerned that the news of your friend's death has been more of a shock than you realize.'

'You think I'm mad.'

'I must tell you that I took the liberty of examining your papers. There was an address in Geneva, and I have written to your father. My recommendation is that you stay here until he arrives to take you home.'

'You will never find [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it. I made it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: him. I made him]] too strong, too swift, too intelligent - qualities I thought befitted a new race of Man, but which have proved equally apt for a Devil.'

Kirkdale looks at me thoughtfully. 'I am concerned that the news of your friend's death has been more of a shock than you realize.'

'You think I'm mad.'

'I must tell you that I took the liberty of examining your papers. There was an address in Geneva, and I have written to your father. My recommendation is that you stay here until he arrives to take you home.'

• 'So I am not under arrest?' — turn to 1236
• 'If I am free to leave, I will make my own way home.' — turn to 1245

## 1246
*(01_N9 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_20i.

In the days that follow, I have to fight a constant battle against the black melancholy that threatens to suck me down. The image of my friend is there whenever I close my eyes. His face was covered when I slid him into the water, but in my dreams he is staring blindly back at me, and as he sinks from sight the mouth opens. At that point I always wake, and often it takes several minutes to remind myself that he was definitely dead.

The cup of life is poisoned forever. Melodramatic, you think? That is how I feel. Although the sun shines upon me as upon the happy and gay of heart, I see around me nothing but a dense and frightful darkness, penetrated by no light but the glimmer of two eyes that burn me with their scrutiny. Sometimes they are the expressive eyes of Henri languishing in death, the dark orbs nearly covered by the lids and the long black lashes that fringed them. But mostly they are the lidless, cloudy eyes of the monster as I first saw them in my workshop in Paris.

• It is time you went home. — turn to 1689

## 1254
*(01_NA · Trust thread -4 to -3)*

For a long time I writhe in a fever, only dimly aware of my surroundings. My lucid moments are few, like a drowning man surfacing and gulping at the air before the water again closes over him. I lie stretched on a wretched bed, wound in perspiration-drenched sheets, surrounded by an endless succession of closing doors, gaolers, jangling, keys, locks, chipped tin cups of water pressed to my parched lips. And the endless flicker as day follows night follows day.

Why do I not die? Death snatches away many children, the only hopes of their doting parents. How many brides and youthful lovers have been one day in the bloom of health and hope, and the next a prey for worms and the decay of the tomb? Of what materials am I made, that I can thus resist so many shocks?

But I am doomed to live. And at last my mind awakes to understanding. Morning light blazes in through the bars of my cell. At first I remember only the sense of a great misfortune having overwhelmed me, but then the memories fall back into place like pieces in a jigsaw. I groan bitterly.

This sound disturbs a woman who is sleeping in a chair beside me. The lines of her face are hard and her tone callously empty of sympathy as she asks me, 'Feeling better now?'

• Speak to her. — turn to 1263
• Ask to see Mr Kirwan. — turn to 1298

For a long time I writhe in a fever, only dimly aware of my surroundings. My lucid moments are few, like a drowning man surfacing and gulping at the air before the water again closes over him. I lie stretched on a wretched bed, wound in perspiration-drenched sheets, surrounded by an endless succession of closing doors, gaolers, jangling, keys, locks, chipped tin cups of water pressed to my parched lips. And the endless flicker as day follows night follows day.

Why do I not die? Death snatches away many children, the only hopes of their doting parents. How many brides and youthful lovers have been one day in the bloom of health and hope, and the next a prey for worms and the decay of the tomb? Of what materials am I made, that I can thus resist so many shocks?

But I am doomed to live. And at last my mind awakes to understanding. Morning light blazes in through the bars of my cell. At first I remember only the sense of a great misfortune having overwhelmed me, but then the memories fall back into place like pieces in a jigsaw. I groan bitterly.

This sound disturbs a woman who is sleeping in a chair beside me. The lines of her face are hard and her tone callously empty of sympathy as she asks me, 'Feeling better now?'

• Speak to her. — turn to 1268
• Ask to see Mr Kirwan. — turn to 1302

## 1263
*(01_NB · Trust thread -4 to -3)*

She is a hired nurse, the wife of one of the turnkeys. I am obscurely aware that she has been attending me throughout my illness, but it is the first time I have felt in the same place and moment as my surroundings.

I start to reply in French, then feel the gears of my mind beginning to turn again. 'How long have I been here?'

'Must be almost two months. I was sure you were for the madhouse.'

'I am better now, I believe. But, remembering the misery and horror of my situation, I'm sorry I ever woke up.'

'Oh, you've been awake, right enough. Just raving the whole time, is all.'

'What did I say?'

She snorts. 'Like I'd know your fancy foreign language. Talking about the poor soul you murdered, I wouldn't wonder.'

• 'His death was on my account, that's true.' — turn to 1272
• 'Fetch Mr Kirwan, please.' — turn to 1298

## 1272
*(01_NC · Trust thread -4 to -3)*

'For that matter,' says the old woman, 'it would be better for you if you were dead, as you're only going to be hung when the next sessions come on, and if you pegged out from fever you'd save the expense of a trial and execution. Still, that's none of my business. I've been told to nurse you and get you fit to be strung up. I do my duty with a clear conscience, and it'd be just as well if everybody could say the same.'

I turn with loathing from the woman who can utter so unfeeling a speech to a person just rescued from the very edge of death. It is a terrible thing to wake from oblivion and have to acknowledge again the harsh truth of tragedy. Henri is dead. That catastrophe cannot be undone. I meant it when I told her I would rather have died too.

• Not until you have revenged yourself. — turn to 1281
• Who will be next to die? — turn to 1290

## 1298
*(01_NF · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

The woman makes a pantomime of looking around the cell. 'Bless me, but I can't see where your servant has scurried off to, so I expect you'll have to wait till Mr Kirwan has time to look in.'

'Take him my message. I'm sure he'll want to know I've recovered my wits.'

'You can thank him for that. A very kind man, is Mr Kirwan, even to the worst sort of scum we get in here. See those bottles of medicine? He's had a physician in every day treating you. At his own expense, I might add.'

I pick up the bottles to examine the labels - almost knocking them to the floor as I do, because of the tremor in my hands.

'Careful,' mutters the old woman peevishly.

'Laudanum! Why not leave me a bottle of gin? Is your local physician also an innkeeper in his spare time?'

That was a mistake. Throwing me a venomous look, the old woman bustles out. The hollow sound as the bolt shoots home is like the single miserable toll of a funeral bell. Despite my opinion of the doctor's prescription, I am curious as to why Kirwan should be so concerned about my health. For who could be interested in the fate of a murderer, but the hangman who would gain his fee?

• You can ask him when he comes to see you. — turn to 1306

## 1306
*(01_NG · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

I am gradually recovering my strength. Today I am sitting up in a chair, though with eyes half open. Gloom and misery weigh heavily on my spirits. Perhaps I should confess to the crime, as Justine did, just to have an end of it.

Such are my thoughts when the door of my room opens. Mr Kirwan joins me. His countenance, as always, is a picture of compassion. He brings a chair close to mine and addresses me in French:

'I fear that this place is very shocking to you, Monsieur Frankenstein. Can I do anything to make you more comfortable?'

'Thank you. It doesn't matter to me one way or the other. I am beyond comforting.'

'I realize that the sympathy of a stranger can be of little relief to one borne down by so strange a misfortune. But you will, I hope, soon quit this melancholy abode. Doubtless evidence can easily be brought to free you from the criminal charge.'

'That is the least of my concerns. I am the most miserable of men. Persecuted as I have been, can death be any worse?'

'That's what Hamlet asked himself, with the mortal coil and so on, wasn't it. No one's ever going to be able to answer that this side of the grave. But what interested me is this talk of persecution. While you were ill, there were quite a few things you said that strike me as puzzling.'

• 'What things?' — turn to 1315
• 'As I have told you, his death was my fault.' — turn to 1324
• 'Why are you keeping me locked up?' — turn to 1333

## 1314
*(01_NG · Trust thread 6)*

I am gradually recovering my strength. Today I am sitting up in a chair, though with eyes half open. Gloom and misery weigh heavily on my spirits. Perhaps I should confess to the crime, as Justine did, just to have an end of it.

Such are my thoughts when the door of my room opens. Mr Kirwan joins me. His countenance, as always, is a picture of compassion. He brings a chair close to mine and addresses me in French:

'I fear that this place is very shocking to you, Monsieur Frankenstein. Can I do anything to make you more comfortable?'

'Thank you. It doesn't matter to me one way or the other. I am beyond comforting.'

'I realize that the sympathy of a stranger can be of little relief to one borne down by so strange a misfortune. But you will, I hope, soon quit this melancholy abode. Doubtless evidence can easily be brought to free you from the criminal charge.'

## 1315
*(01_NH · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'Sometimes you'd be raving about how you'd killed your own brother, and a girl called Justine who you - well, whom you knew, it seems. And even the unfortunate Mr Clerval, whose body was there in that boat.'

'There you are. Condemned out of my own mouth.'

'You're in a dreadful hurry to climb that scaffold, Mr Frankenstein. Because at other times you begged us to help you overcome the fiend - the monster, you called him - who killed all those people.'

'I might as well ask for help in destroying my own shadow.'

'Hmm. But you see, I happen to know that you didn't kill your brother. In fact it was the girl Justine who was convicted of that. It's funny the sort of things people will say. I've been a magistrate long enough to know the truth is never quite on the surface.'

• 'You will have to dig very deep to find the truth in this case.' — turn to 1333

## 1351
*(01_NL · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_28e.

'I gave him ten years' hard labour,' Kirwan goes on. 'Did he so much as blink? Not he. There's more remorse in a rattlesnake. But his father came to see me that night. I could smell the drink off him. A big man, used to hauling great nets filled with fish, but he was weeping like a child. And he was no soft touch, let me tell you. He'd broken a few tavern tables in his time.'

'Like father, like son,' I say, hoping to wind his homely little tale to a close.

'Mr Frankenstein, you're a clever man but you're awful blind with it. Didn't I say the son was cold as a thaw wind? The father had a conscience, though, so all the sins of the young man went onto his bill. That's how he saw it. "I'm to blame, Mr Kirwan," he told me.'

'What did you say?'

'It's not quite so straightforward. A charge was brought, so your case will need to be heard by the county court in a few weeks' time. But I'm confident you'll then be a free man.'

'They may not share your belief in my innocence. I'm not sure I do.'

He smiles, not sure whether I'm joking or not. 'The presiding justice is my brother-in-law. Not that we've discussed the case or anything.'

## 1387
*(01_NP · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

It *is* my father. Nothing could give me greater pleasure than to see his strong, wise countenance. I stretch out my hand. 'You are safe? And Elizabeth?'

'Victor, my boy, of course we are safe. We're going to get this cleared up, don't worry. Kirwan understands. There are a few formalities, but you'll be out of here in no time.' He looks around at the barred windows, the wretched appearance of the room - and, no doubt, the wretched appearance of its occupant. 'A terrible business, what happened to Clerval...'

In my weak state, the name of my unfortunate friend is an agitation too great to be endured. I slump on the bed, weeping. 'Poor Henri. He would be alive if not for me.'

'An unfortunate accident,' says my father, uncomfortable with the display of emotion.

• An accident? How can he call it that? — turn to 1414
• Just go along with what he's saying. — turn to 1423

## 1414
*(01_NS · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'He was strangled, Father! The marks on his neck... like William.'

'Calm down, Victor. This place is hardly conducive to recovery, but I've spoken to Mr Kirwan and we appreciate the severity of the shock you have suffered.'

'I thought we were talking about Henri. The shock, in his case, was fatal.'

'There's no call for sarcasm. I've made some enquiries about Clerval. The general feeling is that he skirted a little close to the wind and paid the price, and if Kirwan is willing to leave it there then I think we should too.'
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_one_28c:

'Oh yes, Father, Kirwan too insinuated something sordid about Henri's activities. But I can tell you that he was the dearest and best man in the world and, as his death was my fault, I'm damned if I'll let his good name be taken from him too.'

My father puts his arm around me, comforting and controlling too. 'No one will say a word against him, Victor,' he says in my ear. 'And you shouldn't blame yourself either. What's past is past, and soon we'll be going home.']][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_one_28c:

'I cannot guess how the demon has contrived this - to rob Henri of his good name as well as his life.'

'I suppose it was a demon that rode him,' says my father thoughtfully. 'At any rate, nobody blames you for what happened. Clerval brought it on himself.']]

## 1423
*(01_NT · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

## 1432
*(01_NU · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_30b.

The season of the assizes approaches. I have already been three months in prison and, although in continual danger of a relapse, I am obliged to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county town where the court is held.

I am spared the disgrace of appearing publicly as a criminal, as the case is not brought before a criminal court. The speed with which they deal with my case, coming after the feverish introspection of long weeks pacing my cell, leaves me bewildered. I am hardly called on to speak. Mr Kirwan has charged himself with every care of collecting witnesses and arranging my defence. The jury rejects the bill on the basis of a sealed affidavit from my father and very soon after I am set free.

As I quit the prison, I hear one of the men say, 'He may be innocent of the murder, but there's no doubt he has a bad conscience.' My father also hears this and, seeing my agitation, tries to distract me on our way to the coach stand with talk of home.

• Tell him about your bad conscience. — turn to 1441
• Ask after Elizabeth. — turn to 1450

## 1440
*(01_NU · Trust thread 6)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_30b.

The season of the assizes approaches. I have already been three months in prison and, although in continual danger of a relapse, I am obliged to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county town where the court is held.

I am spared the disgrace of appearing publicly as a criminal, as the case is not brought before a criminal court. The speed with which they deal with my case, coming after the feverish introspection of long weeks pacing my cell, leaves me bewildered. I am hardly called on to speak. Mr Kirwan has charged himself with every care of collecting witnesses and arranging my defence. The jury rejects the bill on the basis of a sealed affidavit from my father and very soon after I am set free.

As I quit the prison, I hear one of the men say, 'He may be innocent of the murder, but there's no doubt he has a bad conscience.' My father also hears this and, seeing my agitation, tries to distract me on our way to the coach stand with talk of home.

• Tell him about your bad conscience. — turn to 1449
• Ask after Elizabeth. — turn to 1458

## 1441
*(01_NV · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

What that warder said, Father...'

'Tittle-tattle!' he says with a snort. Obviously he's been brooding on it too. 'At least we can leave all that behind us.'

'But he's right, I do have a bad conscience. William, Justine and now Henri all died through my infernal machinations.' He tries to quieten me, but I hear my voice rising. 'And whose death is to finish the tragedy? Oh Father, let's not remain another instant in this wretched country. Take me where I may forget myself, my existence, and all the world.'

'Help you with your bags, sirs?' says the driver as we board the coach for Dublin. 'We'll soon have you out of this wretched country, now, don't you worry.'

• You're going home. — turn to 1459

## 1450
*(01_NW · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'You'll see her soon. And home. Those are tonics as effective as anything you learnt to prescribe in Paris, I wouldn't wonder.'

'I do long to take a boat out on the lake and see the blue water and the snow-capped mountains all around.'

My father is just paying for our coach tickets, but he is so taken aback by my tone that he pauses with the notes still in his hand and turns to look at me. 'You say that with such melancholy, Victor.'

'Because I allowed myself a momentary dream of happiness. The truth is, the prison I have just left is as likely a place for me to find peace now as the loveliest scenery of home. If I were to find a place or person that gave me comfort, I can be sure that [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it will tear them from me.'

'Of what]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he will tear them from me.'

'Of whom]] do you speak? I don't understand.'

'If I had the courage, Father, I should put an end to myself. Existence has become loathsome to me. Happiness is no longer possible. Why, then, not quit this sterile promontory for good?'

The coachman is overseeing the loading of our bags. Looking over his shoulder, he says, 'That's exactly my own feelings about these parts, sir. Don't worry, just a few minutes now and I'll have you safely on the road to Dublin.'

• You're going home. — turn to 1459

## 1459
*(01_NX · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_with_alphonse.

I feel as if I am relieved from a heavy weight when the ship sets out with a fair wind from Ireland. The coast drops away over the rim of the world and I know I am at least quit of the place that has been to me the scene of so much misery.

We share a cabin. I lie awake in the darkness listening to my father snore. It must be gone midnight. The waves smack and slap against the hull, the timbers creak slumbrously, but my mind as ever teems with a thousand notions.

• Why not go up on deck? — turn to 1468
• Rest, and sleep will come. — turn to 1478

## 1468
*(01_NY · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

I stand at the rail looking at the stars and listening to the dashing of the waves. The darkness shuts out any sight of land, for which I am glad. The past appears to me in the light of a frightful dream. Yet the vessel, the sea all around, the straining sails, and the wind that blows me from that detested shore - all speak too forcibly of the inescapable truth. It is no dream. Henri, my friend and dearest companion, is not waiting for me in the cabin below. He has fallen victim to me and the monster of my creation.

Such brooding thoughts prolong a journey that, measured by the clock, takes only a few days, and my pulse beats with a feverish, etiolated joy when we sight the harbour at Le Havre and I reflect that I shall soon see Geneva.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

• Read it. — turn to 1708
• You'll see her soon enough. — turn to 1698

I stand at the rail looking at the stars and listening to the dashing of the waves. The darkness shuts out any sight of land, for which I am glad. The past appears to me in the light of a frightful dream. Yet the vessel, the sea all around, the straining sails, and the wind that blows me from that detested shore - all speak too forcibly of the inescapable truth. It is no dream. Henri, my friend and dearest companion, is not waiting for me in the cabin below. He has fallen victim to me and the monster of my creation.

Such brooding thoughts prolong a journey that, measured by the clock, takes only a few days, and my pulse beats with a feverish, etiolated joy when we sight the harbour at Le Havre and I reflect that I shall soon see Geneva.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

• Read it. — turn to 1711
• You'll see her soon enough. — turn to 1701

## 1478
*(01_NZ · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

My mind, instead of giving me the dreamless sleep I crave, begins to replay my whole life. The days of youthful joy with my family in Geneva. The first glimpse of Elizabeth standing wide-eyed beside the carriage that brought her. The awful, rupturing blow that was the death of my mother. And my feelings of trepidation and excitement on setting out for university.

I am forced to relive the unreasoning fervour that propelled me towards the moment of creation. I see again the watery eye and imbecile smile as my hideous enemy awoke to life, and I call to mind the panic of that first night, pacing the courtyard in the rain.

I cannot hold a train of thought. My mind is a matrix of memories only. A thousand feelings press upon me, and I feel cold tears soaking my face. I reach for the jug of water beside me, and my fingers brush the little brown bottle of laudanum that I have carried with me since that first breakdown in Paris.

• Go up on deck for some fresh air. — turn to 1468
• A dose of laudanum will help quiet your nerves. — turn to 1488

## 1488
*(01_O0 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

Thank you for your advice, but I think I will not add drug addiction to my other problems. Instead I lie on my bunk. Sleep will not come. After many hours in which my mind seems to run in smaller and smaller wheels, a trapped mouse in a maze of undefined fears, I see the sky lightening outside and decide it is time to get up.

After a short voyage we put in at Le Havre.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

• Read it. — turn to 1708
• You'll see her soon enough. — turn to 1698

## 1491
*(01_O0 · Trust thread 1)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

I do find a small quantity of laudanum helps me to get to sleep. Oppressed by morbid visions as I am, perhaps a double dose...

But on this occasion sleep does not afford me respite from thought and misery. My dreams race into the future, presenting a succession of terrible outcomes. Half awake, as the predawn sky pales outside the porthole, I am possessed by a kind of nightmare in which I feel the fiend's grasp on my neck. Tossing to and fro on my bunk, I struggle to break free. Groans and cries ring in my ears.

'Victor! Victor!' My father shakes me to full consciousness. I see him glance at the laudanum bottle, but he says nothing.

After a short voyage we put in at Le Havre.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

Half awake, as the predawn sky pales outside the porthole, I am possessed by a kind of nightmare in which I feel the fiend's grasp on my neck. Tossing to and fro on my bunk, I struggle to break free. Groans and cries ring in my ears.

'Victor! Victor!' My father shakes me to full consciousness. I see him glance at the laudanum bottle, but he says nothing.

After a short voyage we put in at Le Havre.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

• Read it. — turn to 1717
• You'll see her soon enough. — turn to 1707

## 1498
*(01_O1 · Trust thread -4)*

Where am I?' I stop, seeing her look of incomprehension. Of course, I had forgotten I'm in Britain. I repeat the question in English.

'It's Mr Kirkdale's house, sir,' she says, hurrying with her tray to the door.

'How long have I been unwell?'

Already out of the door, she calls back, 'I don't know, sir. I've only been here six weeks myself.'

Six weeks! What enormities might [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the monster]] have wrought in that time? My father. Elizabeth. They are in danger.

## 1508
*(01_O2 · Trust thread -4)*

I swing my legs out of bed, but the effort sends a sharp pain throbbing through my skull. I have to crawl on all fours to the wardrobe. My clothes are hanging there. Soaked in a cold sweat, I lean back against the wall, and that's how Kirkdale finds me.

'My dear fellow,' he says, helping me back to the bed. 'You must take things easy at first. You have been very ill.'

EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the fiend]] said *I will be with you on your wedding night*, so [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he]] cannot mean to murder Elizabeth. Is my father in danger? Perhaps. But as long as I've been lying helpless here in Perth, I don't think [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom would undertake a journey to Geneva.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the creature would undertake a journey to Geneva.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: It gains no satisfaction from its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: He gains no satisfaction from his]] crimes unless I am fit to understand and to suffer.

I look towards the window. It is late afternoon. It must have rained earlier, because there are bright drops on the glass and I can see a faint streak of colour against the sky where the sun struggles to form a rainbow.

It makes me shudder to think [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it is out there in the streets, probably looking up at this very window. But, as long as it is here, at least my family are safe.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he is out there in the streets, probably looking up at this very window. But, as long as it is here, at least my family are safe.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he is out there in the streets, probably looking up at this very window. But, as long as he is here, at least my family are safe.]]

## 1528
*(01_O4 · Trust thread -4)*

Kirkdale draws up a chair beside my bed. 'You have been delirious for some considerable time, Mr Frankenstein. You had us quite worried.'

'It's very kind of you to have looked after me.'

'Think nothing of it. Simple Christian charity.' He pauses, choosing his next words carefully. 'You recall what happened? The shock you received?'

'My friend's murder.'

He nods. 'I'm afraid you've missed the funeral.'

'I wish you could tell me you've apprehended the one responsible.'

'It's very difficult in the case of a stranger,' he says, thinking that I meant to criticize the local constabulary. 'Hard to find witnesses and so forth. And when you couple that with Mr Clerval's predilections...'

## 1604
*(01_OD · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

It *is* my father. Nothing could give me greater pleasure than to see his strong, wise countenance. I clasp his hand in both of mine. His health is not usually good, but he feels robust as a rock compared to my fever-wasted strength.

'Father! You are safe? And Elizabeth?'

'Yes, yes, my boy, we are safe. Of course we are. I'm going to get you home, don't worry. We have berths on a ship to Le Havre sailing tomorrow.' He pauses. A muscle twitches in his jaw. 'A terrible business, what happened to Clerval...'

In my weak state, the name of my unfortunate friend is an agitation too great to be endured. I slump on the bed, weeping. 'Poor Henri. He would be alive if not for me.'

'It was an unfortunate accident,' says my father.

• An accident? How can he call it that? — turn to 1614
• Just go along with what he's saying. — turn to 1624

It *is* my father. Nothing could give me greater pleasure than to see his strong, wise countenance. I clasp his hand in both of mine. His health is not usually good, but he feels robust as a rock compared to my fever-wasted strength.

'Father! You are safe? And Elizabeth?'

'Yes, yes, my boy, we are safe. Of course we are. I'm going to get you home, don't worry. We have berths on a ship to Le Havre sailing tomorrow.' He pauses. A muscle twitches in his jaw. 'A terrible business, what happened to Clerval...'

In my weak state, the name of my unfortunate friend is an agitation too great to be endured. I slump on the bed, weeping. 'Poor Henri. He would be alive if not for me.'

'It was an unfortunate accident,' says my father.

• An accident? How can he call it that? — turn to 1621
• Just go along with what he's saying. — turn to 1631

## 1614
*(01_OE · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'He was strangled, Father! The marks on his neck, black and huge and deep... Like William.'

'Victor, I must tell you that I've made some enquiries about Clerval. The general feeling is that he skirted a little close to the wind and paid the price. Mr Kirkdale has reached the same conclusion.'

'God, what are you saying? How has the demon contrived this? To rob Henri of his good name as well as his life! [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: It]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: He]] is a fiend indeed.'

'I suppose it *was* a demon that rode him,' says my father thoughtfully. 'At any rate, nobody blames you for what happened. Clerval brought it on himself.'

• Now at least you can go home. — turn to 1634

## 1634
*(01_OG · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_with_alphonse.

I feel as if I am relieved from a heavy weight when the ship sets out with a fair wind from Scotland. The coast slides swiftly past and I know I am at least quit of the place that has been to me the scene of so much misery.

We share a cabin. I lie awake in the darkness listening to my father snore. It must be gone midnight. The waves smack and slap against the hull, the timbers creak slumbrously, but my mind as ever teems with a thousand notions.

• Why not go up on deck? — turn to 1468
• Rest, and sleep will come. — turn to 1478

## 1644
*(01_OH · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

The weeks pass slowly. The summer sky is piled with clouds like overhanging crags. During the day, the weather is frequently oppressively close. Thunderstorms blacken the afternoons and turn the sky into an immensity of rattling noise - or so it seems to me, for whom the sun has gone out since Henri's death. Alone in a strange place, I start at every footstep on the path outside at night. When I wake in the night, breathing hard, it is with both dread and hope that I fumble for the candle and look around the unfamiliar room, in case I should find the visitor at my bedside whose coming would end my despair.

At last, in the middle of a sweltering afternoon in which the whole city lies listless and fevered, a carriage stops in front of Mr Kirkdale's house. Down in the street, a familiar figure raises his hand. I smile for the first time since my arrival here, and hurry down to greet my father.

• Talk to him about Henri's death. — turn to 1653
• Ask after Elizabeth. — turn to 1662
• Get home as quickly as possible. — turn to 1634

Alone in a strange place, I start at every footstep on the path outside at night. When I wake in the night, breathing hard, it is with both dread and hope that I fumble for the candle and look around the unfamiliar room, in case I should find the visitor at my bedside whose coming would end my despair.

At last, in the middle of a sweltering afternoon in which the whole city lies listless and fevered, a carriage stops in front of Mr Kirkdale's house. Down in the street, a familiar figure raises his hand. I smile for the first time since my arrival here, and hurry down to greet my father.

• Talk to him about Henri's death. — turn to 1661
• Ask after Elizabeth. — turn to 1670
• Get home as quickly as possible. — turn to 1642

## 1671
*(01_OK · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'He was strangled, Father, exactly like William. And by the same foul hand.'

'Victor, I must tell you that I've made some enquiries about Clerval. He was one of those men who led another life. Mr Kirkdale has reached the same conclusion.'

'Then you have both got it entirely wrong. Henri's friendship with me was the cause of his death.'

'I hope,' says my father gravely, 'that you don't know what you are saying. You were like two brothers, it always seemed to me, and what on earth is wrong with that. A simple, wholesome friendship.'

He refuses to be drawn further on the matter. As usual for my father, he has said either too little or too much.

• Now at least you can go home. — turn to 1634

## 1680
*(01_OL · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'It is a tragedy that I wasn't here,' I say. 'To think of him, set upon and murdered. I weep to think of the terror and confusion he must have felt in those last moments.'

My father takes my hand. It's a gesture that belongs to my childhood. After six years in Paris I am a different person, and after a moment of embarrassment he lets go.

'I merely thank God you were not with him,' he says.

• Now at least you can go home. — turn to 1634

## 1689
*(01_OM · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

I set sail for Le Havre, not wishing to revisit any of the places where I enjoyed a few moments of tranquillity with my beloved Henri. It would be dreadful to see again any of the people we visited together, who would be bound to reopen the wound left by his death, even if they should remain silent about his absence.

On arrival I show the port official my papers under signs with the words *Havre de Marat* freshly painted out. The Revolution has cooled, the counter-revolution met with grapeshot outside the Tuileries, and all the while the French bureaucracy has quietly kept the store open.

There is a parcel of letters waiting for me at the coaching inn, including several from Elizabeth. The latest, dated only ten days earlier, is the longest.

• Read it. — turn to 1708
• You'll see her soon enough. — turn to 1698

## 1708
*(01_OP · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

'My dearest friend,' she begins,

'It gave me the greatest pleasure to receive a letter [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_with_alphonse: from my uncle]]to say you are on your way home. You are no longer at a formidable distance, and I may hope to see you in less than a fortnight. My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered! I expect to see you looking even more ill than when you quitted Geneva. These last months have been passed most miserably, tortured as I have been by anxious suspense. Yet I hope to see peace in your countenance, and to find that your heart is not totally void of comfort and tranquillity.

'Yet I fear that the same feelings now exist that made you so miserable a year ago, even perhaps augmented by time. I would not disturb you at this period when so many misfortunes weigh upon you, but a conversation that I had with my uncle [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_with_alphonse: prior to his departure]]renders some explanation necessary before we meet.

'Explanation! you may possibly say. What can Elizabeth have to explain? If you really say this, my questions are answered, and I have no more to do than to sign myself your affectionate cousin. But you are distant from me, and it is possible that you may dread and yet be pleased with what I am going to say. As I think this is probably the case, I dare not any longer postpone writing what, during your absence, I have often wished to express to you, but have never had the courage to begin.'

• Read on. — turn to 1718
• Leave it. You'll see her in a few weeks. — turn to 1698

## 1718
*(01_OQ · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_43a.

'You well know, Victor, that our union has been the favourite plan of your parents ever since our infancy. We were told this when young, and taught to look forward to it as an event that would certainly take place. We were affectionate playmates during childhood, and dear and valued friends to one another as we grew older. But as brother and sister often entertain a lively affection towards each other without desiring a more intimate union, may not such also be our case? Tell me, dearest Victor. Answer me honestly, for our mutual happiness is at stake. Do you love another?

'You have travelled; you have spent several years of your life in Paris. I confess to you, my friend, that when I saw you last year so unhappy, so desirous of solitude, flying from the company of your family, I could not help supposing that you might regret our connection. Perhaps you believe yourself bound in honour to fulfil the wishes of your parents. But this is false reasoning. I confess to you, my cousin, that I love you, and that in my airy dreams of futurity you have been my constant friend and companion. But it is your happiness I desire as well as – ' She's crossed that out and put *more than* ' – my own. Thus I declare to you that our marriage would render me eternally miserable unless it were of your own free choice. Even now I weep to think that, borne down as you are by the cruellest misfortunes, you might stifle all hope of that love and happiness which would alone restore you to yourself, simply because you believe that to wed me is your duty. And so that I, who have so strong an affection for you, may increase your miseries tenfold by being an obstacle to your true wishes.

'Ah! Victor, be assured that your cousin and playmate sincerely loves you, and it would make me miserable to trap you in matrimony against the wishes of your heart. Be happy, my friend; and if you obey me in this one request, remain satisfied that nothing on earth will have the power to interrupt my tranquillity.

'Do not let this letter disturb you. Do not answer tomorrow, or the next day, or even until you come, if it will give you pain. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_with_alphonse: My uncle will send me news of your health, and if]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_with_alphonse: If]] I see but one smile on your lips when we meet, occasioned by this or any other exertion of mine, I shall need no other happiness.

'Elizabeth Lavenza.'

• The poor girl. — turn to 1728
• It's brave of her to write that letter. — turn to 1738
• How do you feel about what she's written? — turn to 1748

## 1758
*(01_OU · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_one_43e.

My reply is calm and affectionate. 'I fear, my beloved girl,' I write, 'little happiness remains for us on earth. Yet all that I may one day enjoy is centred on you. Chase away your idle fears. To you alone do I consecrate my life and my [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: hopes of happiness]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 0: endeavours for contentment]]. I have one secret, Elizabeth - a dreadful one. When you hear it, far from being surprised at my melancholy, you will only wonder that I can survive what I have endured. I will confide this tale of misery and terror to you the day after our wedding - for, my sweet cousin, there must be perfect confidence between us. But until then, I ask that you not mention or allude to it. This I most earnestly entreat, and I know you will comply.'

I give the letter to the postmaster. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_with_alphonse: My father looks at his watch for the third or fourth time. 'Did you write her a whole book?' he says, nonetheless pleased. 'Come along, Victor, our coach will be leaving.']][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_with_alphonse: Outside, the coach driver is ringing his bell.]]

My reply is calm and affectionate. 'I fear, my beloved girl,' I write, 'little happiness remains for us on earth. Yet all that I may one day enjoy is centred on you. Chase away your idle fears. To you alone do I consecrate my life and my [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: hopes of happiness]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 0: endeavours for contentment]]. I have one secret, Elizabeth - a dreadful one. When you hear it, far from being surprised at my melancholy, you will only wonder that I can survive what I have endured. I will confide this tale of misery and terror to you the day after our wedding - for, my sweet cousin, there must be perfect confidence between us. But until then, I ask that you not mention or allude to it. This I most earnestly entreat, and I know you will comply.'

I give the letter to the postmaster. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_with_alphonse: My father looks at his watch for the third or fourth time. 'Did you write her a whole book?' he says, nonetheless pleased. 'Come along, Victor, our coach will be leaving.']][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_with_alphonse: Outside, the coach driver is ringing his bell.]]

• Continue your journey. — turn to 1704

## 1807
*(01_OZ · Trust thread -4 to -1)*

After one period of protracted silence, as we go juddering and rattling up a rutted track that connects two highways, my father says, 'There is no need to feel ashamed of your appearance before that court, Victor. Perhaps you feel some stain yet attaches to your character, but the judges were at pains to exonerate you fully.'

I am not much in a mood to talk, having had enough of his attempts to draw me out of myself, and I fear that if I answer him it will be ill-temperedly.

• Pretend to be asleep. — turn to 1918
• Tell him honestly what you think. — turn to 1816

## 1825
*(01_P1 · Trust thread -4 to -1)*

'A very unfortunate affair,' says my father. 'Still, we can look forward to happier times, eh? Look, Victor, there is a sign to Dijon. Not far now. Elizabeth will be waiting eagerly by the window every morning, if I know her.'

He seems content to ride on in silence, so I settle my head back and try to get some sleep.

• He's right, you'll be home in a few days. — turn to 1918

## 1834
*(01_P2 · Trust thread 2)*

'What do you mean, Victor?' he cries desperately. 'You keep making assertions of this sort. Are you mad? I entreat you, son, never to say anything of this kind ever again.'

Usually when I make an outburst like this, he attributes it to delirium and the madness of grief. Occasionally he has pressed me to say more - even then, I think, more to draw the poison of what he considers insanity than out of any suspicion that I might speak the truth. Until now I have retreated into silence, convinced that, if I were to tell him about the wretch I created, he would certainly think I have lost my wits.

'Father,' I say bitterly, 'I would give the whole world to reveal to you the fatal secret, but I would spare you that horror.'

• You're wise to keep silent. — turn to 1840
• Perhaps it's time you told him. — turn to 1846

## 1840
*(01_P3 · Trust thread 2)*

I must strive to be calm. It is enough that I am conscious of my own transgressions. It helps no one if I rant about them incoherently. And so I sit and bite my tongue, literally, until it bleeds, and so curb the imperious voice of wretchedness, which yearns to declare itself to the whole world.

After a while my father says, 'I must say, Victor, you seem more contented than I have seen you since the trip to Chamounix. Look, there is a sign to Dijon. I didn't realize we'd come so far. Elizabeth will be waiting eagerly by the window every morning, if I know her.'

He seems content to ride on in silence, so I settle my head back and try to get some sleep.

• You'll be home in a few days. — turn to 1921

## 1846
*(01_P4 · Trust thread 2)*

'I am not mad. The sun can bear witness. The sky knows I am telling the truth. I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations. I would rather have shed my own blood, drop by drop, a thousand times if I could have saved their lives. But I could not, Father. Indeed, I could not sacrifice the whole human race.'

After a long pause, my father responds cheerfully enough, changing the subject to point out the road signs and how near we are to home. But I see the pain and worry in his eyes, convinced as he must be now that I have become deranged, and I feel a fresh twist of self-loathing that I have burdened him with that too.

• Better continue the journey in silence. — turn to 1921

But I see the pain and worry in his eyes, convinced as he must be now that I have become deranged, and I feel a fresh twist of self-loathing that I have burdened him with that too.

• Better continue the journey in silence. — turn to 1922

## 1861
*(01_P6 · Trust thread -4 to -1)*

'I know you felt Justine to be innocent. It's natural. She was part of our household for years. Indeed, there were times in your youth that I thought you preferred her company to your cousin's.'

'It isn't mere sentiment, Father, that makes me protest her innocence. She died by my machinations, as surely as if I had built the gallows on which she was hanged. You may believe I would have put my own head in the noose if it could have saved Henri's life, but I could not. Nor could I doom the human race, though one deed of mine would spare this family future misery.'

'What do you mean?'

I stare out at the woods rushing past the carriage, noting distantly that it will not be long before the leaves turn. 'A man may commit a dreadful deed believing he does good. Macbeth thought he would make a better king than Duncan, perhaps. But then another must be sacrificed to cover up the crime. And another - no self-delusion now can hide the truth.'

He turns to me, tight lines of worry across his face. 'Victor, what are you saying?'

'I cannot fix what I've done. But one monster is better than an entire species. I will see an end of it, Father. And because I refuse to compound my crimes, Henri is dead.'

• Enough. He already thinks you're mad. — turn to 1825

*(01_P7 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

Oh, that I could wind back time, each league taking me back a month, so that I should arrive in Geneva eighteen years old and innocent.

When I get back, I'll have to go and see Henri's family. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > -2: It will be the hardest thing about my homecoming.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ -2: Perhaps I can leave it a while. Or send Elizabeth - she'll have a better idea what to say to them.]]

There is the signpost for Beaune. Less than thirty leagues to go now.

• You'll soon be home. — turn to 1925

## 1889
*(01_P9 · Trust thread -4 to -2)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_two_11.

What? Having plundered the secrets of Life, now I should conquer Time? Hah! And then bring back the dead, if I still had an idle moment before bedtime? Ha ha, that is a fine jest!

The coachman slides back the partition. 'Are you all right, sir?'

It's absurd - inside, my heart is black as pitch, and here I am rolling merrily on the seat like a drunk coming back from the theatre. With a supreme effort I pull myself together.

'I am fine. How far to our next stop, citizen?'

'We'll be at Beaune in a couple of hours, sir.'

'A nice wine with supper tonight, then. Thank you, citizen.'

Before closing the panel, he says, 'No need for "citizen" these days, sir.

• You'll soon be home. — turn to 1918

Oh God, I'll have to go and see [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_two_11 or you have KW_e_two_12: his]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_two_11 and you do not have KW_e_two_12: Henri's]]family. How will I face them? In case I had not reason enough to despise my own wretchedness, I'm inflicting years of distress on them. They will vainly wait for him to come home, the sands of their hope slowly trickling away. Although I've heard it said that a mother can sense when her child dies. It's better if that's so.

A signpost flashes by: a familiar crossroads. Geneva is less than a hundred miles away now.

• You'll soon be home. — turn to 1924

*(01_PE · Trust thread -4 to -1)*

[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_one_43a: Thank you, I had not forgotten.]]I greet her with a smile and a kiss, with looks and endearments giving the impression that I have thought of none but her since we last parted.

'Oh, dearest cousin,' she says, pressing her cheek to mine, and I taste a salty wetness on my lips. 'You remembered my letter.'

'[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_one_43a: I have read it a hundred times,' I assure her, noting over her shoulder the pleasure this remark gives my father.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_one_43a: How could I forget?' I reply, casting about for some way to change the subject.]]

• How do you feel about being home? — turn to 1948

## 1948
*(01_PF · Trust thread -4 to -1)*

It's not easy. The cosy familiarity of my surroundings, which I had expected to soothe away the nightmares, in fact throws the events of the last few months into still more terrible relief. The worst moments are the most commonplace - when I sit at the breakfast table and hear the inexorable soft ticking of the clock, or notice that old crack across the tile inside the back door, or watch Elizabeth at [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: her tireless]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 0: the unending Penelopean work of her]] embroidery under the apple tree in the garden.

I feel as though I am burning with rage, but that the fire is pouring into an immense cold sea, so that in the end my thoughts churn darkly but I only sit silent and despondent, unaware of place and time.

• You must try to control your moods. — turn to 1958
• Take a walk across the hills. — turn to 1967

## 1967
*(01_PH · Trust thread -5 to -1)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_three_1e.

Leaving the house one morning, I find Elizabeth already dressed for a long hike. 'Exercise will do you good, Victor,' she says, taking my arm.

I must say she is right. Not that striding across the hills dispels the multitude of miseries that beset me, but this is the same landscape that inspired me to miraculous endeavours before. The helplessness is gone. Danger remains, but I recall who I am. Frankenstein! I created life! I have my rage and I will be revenged on the mean wretch that thinks to degrade me like [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: itself]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: himself]].

I am muttering under my breath. I see Elizabeth's sidelong look. 'Not madness, my dear,' I assure her. 'Inspiration.'

• And what about preparations for the wedding? — turn to 1976

## 1976
*(01_PI · Trust thread -5 to -1)*

My father also wishes to discuss that. One day after lunch he asks me into his study to talk about the future. 'I have bought you a house near Cologny,' he tells me, affecting to make light of it but secretly hoping for expressions of delight.

[[If Empathy > -1, read the following:]]

'Father, this is marvellous!' I say, forcing a tone of gaiety into my voice.'

[[If Empathy ≤ -1, read the following:]]

'Thank you, that will be very convenient.'
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_three_1e:

'I've seen how you still enjoy long walks in the country. And]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_three_1e:

'You always enjoyed the countryside, and]] at the same time you'll be near enough that we can see each other every day.'

[[If Empathy > 3, read the following:]]

'Perhaps not every day until after the honeymoon, eh, Father?'

[[If Empathy ≤ 3, read the following:]]

'I could not ask for a more perfect arrangement, Father.'

'You are looking forward to the wedding, then?'

One of his probing questions. He pretends to fill his pipe while actually keeping a close eye on my reaction. How do I answer that honestly, knowing that a frightful fiend doth close behind me tread, and has chosen that day for our fateful assignation?

• Best to say nothing. — turn to 1985
• You can tell a white lie, surely? — turn to 1994

## 2021
*(01_PO · Trust thread -5 to -1)*

As the period fixed for our marriage draws near, whether from cowardice or a sense of helpless inevitability, I feel my heart sink within me. When I'm with my father, I affect a bluff manner that entirely deceives him. He is beaming with joy as he helps with arrangements for the ceremony.

Elizabeth, though, sees a little deeper. I feel her eyes on me, sensing the troubled thoughts that I am concealing behind a mask of happiness. She seems to look forward to our union with placid contentment, but it must be mingled with a little fear[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -1: just as a horse picks up nervousness from its rider.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ -1: , which past misfortunes have surely impressed on her, that what seems to be our certain and tangible joy might dissipate into an airy dream, and leave no trace but deep and everlasting regret.]]

**END OF CHAPTER TWO**

• CHAPTER THREE — turn to 2030

## 2066
*(01_PU · Trust thread -5 to -1)*

Unable to sleep, I finally give up the attempt and rise as predawn turns the sky pale. Throughout the morning I am content to be moved about according to the plans that have been made for me. There is an unreal sense about the house, festooned as it is with streamers of coloured paper and with fluttering womenfolk in every room. I catch my father's eye as we tie each other's cravats. How happy he looks.

After the ceremony, which takes place at midday, a large party assembles at my father's. I hear myself telling face after unfamiliar face that Elizabeth and I will be going to Evian this afternoon. 'We'll spend the night there,' she says, coming over to take my arm. 'And then go back to our house at Cologny tomorrow.'

'It's a fine day,' replies a man who I think may be an uncle. 'Will you go by boat?'

'Oh yes,' says Elizabeth, her face lighting up as she seizes the opportunity she's been waiting for, 'my husband loves sailing.'

[[If Empathy > -1, read the following:]]

She takes great pride in saying it, and I feel guilty that my deliberations about what is to come keep me at a distance, a sleepwalker in the midst of the revelry.

When we get out on the water the sun is bright. It's perhaps the last day like this we'll get this year. The banks of the lake are patterned with the changing hues of autumn, fading into the distant line of blue mountains with their caps of brilliant white.

Elizabeth is watching me from under the shade of a canopy. I stand at the rail, scanning the water for sight of [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: the fiend that]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: the enemy who]] could be lurking there.

• She's waiting for you to say something. — turn to 2075
• Stay alert. There'll be time to talk later. — turn to 2100

## 2075
*(01_PV · Trust thread -5 to -1)*

I take her hand. 'You are quiet, Elizabeth.'

'Because you are, my love.'

This has been her mood throughout the day. There will be joy in her eyes for a moment, continually darkening behind a look of pensive reverie.
[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_four_3:

'Last night at dinner you seemed sorrowful.]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_four_3:

'Lately I have sensed a melancholy behind your smiles.]]But if you knew what I have suffered - and what I may yet have to endure - you would strive to let me taste the freedom from despair that this one afternoon affords me.'

'Be happy, my dear Victor. There is nothing to distress you. Even if a lively joy is not painted in my face, my heart is contented. True, for days I have felt a growing sense of dread. Something whispers to me not to depend too much on the prospect that is opened before us. But I will not listen to such a sinister voice.'

• This is the moment to tell her everything. — turn to 2084
