Elizabeth laughs. 'You are right, beloved. It's an undiscovered land we are sailing to - '

'Evian. There be dragons.'

She laughs again, her mood visibly lightening. 'Matrimony! And we have no map or chart to help us navigate its climes, which no doubt explains why I have been unwontedly fretful. But it will be a land of many summers, Victor.'

'Look how fast we're going, Victor. We'll get to the inn and they won't have our rooms ready. I mean our room. Oh, see those clouds! That big one, it's rolling back from us. A moment ago you couldn't see the peak of Mont Blanc and now the cloud seems balanced on it. I think it's the weather that makes this scenery so interesting, because it is never the same. People think of mountains as unchanging, but I could watch them for hours and be entertained as much as at the theatre. Oh my, look, darling! Look at all the fish! The water's so clear you can see every pebble at the bottom. Did we bring any food to give them? What a shame. But it's a divine day, the most perfect day of the year. Or ever. How blissfully serene all of nature appears at this moment!'

## 2124
*(01_Q1 · Trust thread -6 to -1)*

The wind dies at sunset to a light breeze. The soft air just ruffles the water and causes a pleasant stir among the treetops as we approach the shore. A delightful scent of flowers and hay hangs in the air.

We walk for a short time on the shore, enjoying the transitory light while our bags are carried into the inn. As night falls we have dinner with the curtains open, providing us with an awe-inspiring backdrop of water, woods, and mountains, obscured in darkness, yet still displaying their black outlines.

We are alone in the dining room, though there are candles lit on every table. I look across to a floor-length mirror where a newly married couple dine in silence. Are they happy, I wonder.

As the waiter withdraws having poured our wine, Elizabeth slides her hand across the tablecloth, her fingertips just resting on mine. 'This meal is delicious, Victor, but I'm so excited I can hardly taste it.'

Knowing what is to come, I have hardly touched the food on my own plate.

## 2140
*(01_Q4 · Trust thread -6 to -1)*

> Note the keyword KW_e_five_2.

The wind has started to pick up. Clouds sweep across the face of the moon, darkening the evening, which had seemed so tranquil before. The lake becomes choppy. Suddenly a heavy burst of rain lashes the windowpanes, causing us both to jump.

I have been calm up till now, I have surprised myself with my calm, but as night blurs the edges of things, a thousand fears rouse in my mind. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_three_5b: I slip a hand inside my coat. The pistol is still there.]]Whatever lies ahead, I will sell my life dearly. Either I or the monster will die tonight.

Elizabeth casts me a timid look as we go through to the parlour. When she speaks, it is with downcast face, and so quietly that I almost don't hear her. 'What agitates you, dear Victor? What is it you fear?'

The answer bursts from me. 'Oh! Peace, peace, my love. This night only, and all will be safe. But this night is dreadful, very dreadful.'

A servant brings us brandies and coffee. Mine sit beside me untouched. When the clock strikes, I realize we have been sitting here for an hour. Elizabeth is watching me from the other side of the hearth.

'It is late, dearest,' she says softly.

Following her gaze, I catch a glimpse of the servant who is waiting in the hall for us to go to bed.

• Tell her you'll be up shortly. — turn to 2156
• Go up with her. — turn to 2164

EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_three_5b: I slip a hand inside my coat. The pistol is still there.]]Whatever lies ahead, I will sell my life dearly. Either I or the monster will die tonight.

Elizabeth casts me a timid look as we go through to the parlour. When she speaks, it is with downcast face, and so quietly that I almost don't hear her. 'What agitates you, dear Victor? What is it you fear?'

The answer bursts from me. 'Oh! Peace, peace, my love. This night only, and all will be safe. But this night is dreadful, very dreadful.'

A servant brings us brandies and coffee. Mine sit beside me untouched. When the clock strikes, I realize we have been sitting here for an hour. Elizabeth is watching me from the other side of the hearth.

'It is late, dearest,' she says softly.

Following her gaze, I catch a glimpse of the servant who is waiting in the hall for us to go to bed.

• Tell her you'll be up shortly. — turn to 2157
• Go up with her. — turn to 2165

## 2167
*(01_Q9 · Trust thread 2)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

We ascend to our room. I am tense, eyes restlessly probing the shadows for the furtive movement of the one I fear. Though how could [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it conceal its hulking presence among the low, narrow passages and groaning floorboards of this ancient building? Perhaps it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: he conceal his hulking presence among the low, narrow passages and groaning floorboards of this ancient building? Perhaps he]] will not come after all.

Elizabeth takes my hand. She wears a radiant smile. 'You are trembling, my love,' she says, 'come here into the bedroom where it's warm.'

I stand by the small fireplace, hearing [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_five_3: the small whispering movements of fabric as she gets ready for bed in the adjoining room]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_five_3: the importunate blustering of wind and rain against the tiny leaded panes]]. The door to the dressing room opens. Elizabeth stands there with the lamp behind her. Through the thin cotton of her nightdress I see that she is very slender, barely sturdier than a child. A woman's day clothes conceal that. The female forms I have seen naked, whether dead or living, have usually been lower-class women, and they are always fleshier. And her skin - it's so taut. I know better than anybody what a rig of capillaries and bone and meat and nerve fibres must fit under that skin. It seems miraculous that it could all be packed so perfectly in so delicate a frame.

I am advancing towards the bed when I feel a gust of cold air from under the door. The fire flattens and jumps in the grate. I know what it means. A door or window has been opened downstairs.

• Go to investigate. — turn to 2172
• Stay with your wife. — turn to 2177

Elizabeth stands there with the lamp behind her. Through the thin cotton of her nightdress I see that she is very slender, barely sturdier than a child. A woman's day clothes conceal that. The female forms I have seen naked, whether dead or living, have usually been lower-class women, and they are always fleshier. And her skin - it's so taut. I know better than anybody what a rig of capillaries and bone and meat and nerve fibres must fit under that skin. It seems miraculous that it could all be packed so perfectly in so delicate a frame.

## 2177
*(01_QB · Trust thread 2)*

Elizabeth stretches out on the bed, her hair spread across the pillows, feet together and arms laid out beside her as if she were on a cross. A smile plays on her lips, meek and yet promising a smouldering heat. With half-closed eyes she watches me stoke the fire.

'Are you coming to bed?' It's really just a breath of words, barely audible.

Fearful of relaxing my guard, I cross to lock the door. [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_three_5b: Onto the bedside table I unload my arsenal of defences - the knife, gun and flask of acid. Elizabeth gives a thick, slightly nervous laugh. 'Was that in case I tried]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_three_5b: Elizabeth giggles. 'Is that in case I try]] to get away?'

I'm beside the bed. She doesn't move a muscle, just looks up. I'm reaching for her when -

An explosion of glass. I sense a blur of movement, something huge leaping into the room, but before I can raise my eyes I feel a crunching blow. My teeth grind together. A metallic taste in my mouth. A blossom of spreading red darkness behind my eyes. And over the roar of my own heartbeat I seem to hear, from the top of a deep well, the faint frenzied cry of my bride.

• [If you do not have KW_demonize] Alas, the monster kept his promise. — turn to 2187
• [If you have KW_demonize] Alas, the monster kept its promise. — turn to 2187

I thrust my head indoors and scream for help. A servant is already there with a candle in her hand. 'Oh, sir,' she says, putting her hand to her mouth. 'Your poor wife.'

[[If Empathy < -4, read the following:]]

'Fetch some men with guns,' I snap back. 'The killer is outside!'

The innkeeper is behind her on the stairs. I have to shake him to get him to listen, but eventually he rounds up two or three men with muskets. As they are pulling overcoats and boats on over their nightgowns, the innkeeper's wife comes hesitantly down the stairs. 'It's Madame Frankenstein...' she says.

'Murdered, yes.' I cherish my knot of cold fury. 'And I mean to catch the murderer this very night.'

## 2256
*(01_QN · Trust thread -6 to -1)*

We take boats out onto the lake. Nets are cast, but in vain. After several hours the moon is close to setting and we are forced to return. I see from the sullen faces that most of my companions believe it to be a wild goose chase. After we have landed, a man who I am later told is one of the town councillors takes it upon himself to organize search parties to scour the woods and vineyards by torchlight.

I don't accompany them. I am exhausted, and robbed of my resolve by the knowledge that the monster could lie for an hour on the lake bed, or cling to the freezing heights of one of the surrounding mountains.

Returning to the inn, I cannot make myself climb the stairs to our - to my room. A film seems to descend over my vision. I feel hot and feverish. I sink onto a couch. The fire has gone out in the grate and a chill creeps deep into my bones, but I do not stir. The cup of life is poisoned. I taste the dregs and wonder why death is so unmerciful as to leave me untouched.

Hardly conscious, yet not sleeping, I lie waiting for the dawn of a terrible day, and my eyes restlessly wander the room, as if to seek something I have lost.

**END OF PART FIVE**

Search parties are sent out to scour the lake and surrounding woods. I don't go with them. I am exhausted, and robbed of any hope by the knowledge that the monster could lie for an hour on the lake bed, or cling to the freezing heights of one of the surrounding mountains.

I drive them all from the room. I feel hot and feverish, though the fire has gone out and cold is creeping into the room from the open window. I lie down beside Elizabeth on what was to have been our marriage bed. The cup of life with which we toasted each other is poisoned now. Why is death so unmerciful as to leave me untouched? Why cannot this be the bier on which we two are laid to rest together?

Hardly conscious, yet not sleeping, I await the dawn of a terrible day, and my eyes restlessly wander the room, as if to seek something I have lost.

**END OF PART FIVE**

# PART SIX — THE GREATNESS OF HIS FALL

## 2272
*(01_QQ · Trust thread -6 to -1)*

[ILLUSTRATION: pic6_1.jpg]

*I seek no sympathies, nor need;
The thorns which I have reap'd are of the tree
I planted: they have torn me, and I bleed:
I should have known what fruit would spring from such a seed.*

**CHAPTER ONE**
*Wandering Ministers of Vengeance*

I have hired rowers for the return trip because there is still a strong wind from the west. The fish too are unchanged, slipping through the net of rippled light just as they were [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_e_four_8: when Elizabeth pointed them out]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_e_four_8: yesterday]]. How can so monumental a change have taken place and reality takes no notice?

The bracing tang of the lake air. The autumnal patchwork of the shores. The watery dawn, with the white sun a shivering droplet balanced on the grey teeth of the mountains. The creak and splash of the oars. The fragments of the world are all present but, like a shattered vase pieced together with glue, it fulfils its function only. The thing itself has gone. I have lived through the boiling point of guilt, the freezing point of fear, and finally reached an absolute zero in which nothing stirs, no change is possible, the needle of hope no longer flickers.

In the belly of the boat she lies under a sheet, rocks from the inn's garden weighting the corners. I notice one of the men staring uncomfortably. Her hand has rolled free, as white as a chalk drawing against the dark planks, but showing a pinprick glint of colours as the rocking of the boat tilts her ring into the sun. It was my mother's, promised to Elizabeth since childhood.

• It should stay here in the lake forever. — turn to 2280
• Will you bury it with her? — turn to 2288

## 2283
*(01_QS · Trust thread 2)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

The ring flashes in the early light, rotating twice in the water before it slides out of the sun towards the murkier depths where trembling shade envelops it. My last glimpse is the diamond setting gleaming greenly as it settles on the brown Archaean skin of a rock. A single image, sharpened by the lens of the clear water, and then it is behind us, as irrecoverable as a moment in time.

I will live and die. A billion souls, or a billion billion, will come and go. And her ring will become the heart of a new rock - the geological evidence that we were here, and loved. And one day the Earth will break apart and that rock will be a meteor plummeting towards other suns. That vision seems more real to me, because more definite, than the events of the next twenty-four hours, when the terrible cacophonous din of emotion must surely drown out anything as frangible as bare facts.

• The news will be hard on your father. — turn to 2306

## 2297
*(01_QV · Trust thread 1)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

It's a story spun to quieten childish nightmares. Grandpa isn't dead, he bobs on a cloud and sups on milk and honey. No one really believes any of that. They maintain the fabrication because they fear to see the true face of the universe, unmasked by human lies. *This* was the life I was given. There will be no other. And the only consummation I wish for is blissful oblivion.

→ Turn to 2305.

*(01_QW · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I'm back at the house. I don't remember whether I walked or took a carriage after the boat docked. They are bringing Elizabeth's body here, I know that. The lawn is still strewn with the debris of the wedding breakfast. A string of coloured paper flags, hanging lank in the dew. An ashtray with the squashed stubs of cigars nestled in damp ash. A champagne coupe lies trodden into the flower bed. Amazingly, it seems unbroken, a perfect crystal of aqueous brilliance in the blue shadows under the bushes.

## 2311
*(01_QX · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

As soon as I pull it out of the earth, the fracture is revealed and the glass falls apart. It was only whole until touched. Placing the pieces carefully on the patio wall, I turn to the house. I can't put it off any longer. My father is called by a servant and I meet him on the stairs in his dressing gown. He must read all of the dreadfulness of what I have to say in my face, but still we are forced like puppets to enact the whole confusion of explanations and tears. As the hubbub of grief spreads through the household, I experience a strange sense that last night's calamity was merely the dislodging of a few rocks, and it is only by incautiously spreading the news that I have now triggered the avalanche.

Time passes. I'm hardly aware of day and night. There must be arrangements for Elizabeth's funeral. Visitors come with condolences or papers to sign, and I receive them, as my father has been struck almost senseless with sorrow. At mealtimes he sits while his soup gets cold, eyes drifting vacantly and from time to time looking sharply toward some innocuous disturbance - the chiming of the clock, the entry of a servant.

I often wake now at odd hours of the night, and can only subdue the torment of my thoughts by walking in the garden. Returning from such an excursion, I notice a light on under my father's study door. The clock is striking three in the morning.

• You must talk to him. — turn to 2327
• Everyone grieves in their own way. — turn to 2351

• Everyone grieves in their own way. — turn to 2355

## 2324
*(01_QY · Trust thread 4)*

I meet him on the stairs in his dressing gown. He must read all of the dreadfulness of what I have to say in my face, but still we are forced like puppets to enact the whole confusion of explanations and tears. As the hubbub of grief spreads through the household, I experience a strange sense that last night's calamity was merely the dislodging of a few rocks, and it is only by incautiously spreading the news that I have now triggered the avalanche.

Time passes. I'm hardly aware of day and night. There must be arrangements for Elizabeth's funeral. Visitors come with condolences or papers to sign, and I receive them, as my father has been struck almost senseless with sorrow. At mealtimes he sits while his soup gets cold, eyes drifting vacantly and from time to time looking sharply toward some innocuous disturbance - the chiming of the clock, the entry of a servant.

I often wake now at odd hours of the night, and can only subdue the torment of my thoughts by walking in the garden. Returning from such an excursion, I notice a light on under my father's study door. The clock is striking three in the morning.

## 2343
*(01_R1 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

Then, coming further into the room, I see the long trickle of saliva on his lips. One eye is watching me, the other droops sleepily. That whole side of his face is slack. He utters a nerveless, inarticulate but heartfelt moan that eerily sends my mind back to the attic laboratory in Paris.

I must spend several minutes trying to help him from his chair before I think to rouse a servant. We get Father onto the chaise longue and I open a vein to drain off the excess blood that must be pressing on his brain. I hold the basin myself, kneeling beside him until a pallid grey dawn intrudes between the drapes. My father heaves a sigh. The weak trickle of blood dies away altogether, and I see he is no longer breathing.

→ Turn to 2359.

## 2351
*(01_R2 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I retire to bed, but if I sleep at all it can only be for a few minutes. An anaemic dawn barely penetrates the curtains. I'm roused to full wakefulness by urgent conversation downstairs, the clatter of feet on the stairs. One of the servants is knocking on my door.

'I'll come at once,' I tell her.

'Oh sir, it's your father...'

But I don't need her to tell me. He lost his niece, who was more than a daughter, and with her went all pretence that our family could hope for a future. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -1: The truth is scathing and man cannot live under its glare. At any rate, he could not.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ -1: He could not live under the horrors that have accumulated around us.]]

• There will be another funeral, then. — turn to 2359

## 2359
*(01_R3 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

Are there two funerals, or one? Elizabeth and my father must be buried on different days, but they blur together. I'm back at the house. Listen to that deep silence. No servants, you see; I sent them away. The clock has run down and I've lost track of time. Somewhere along the way it slipped its traces and left me distraught and stranded.

At times I am in a flower-filled meadow and Henri and Elizabeth are with me. A blizzard of blossom tumbles through the air and we are laughing. But they are children again, in fact only a lantern-play of children, and the meadow is memory. Over the next hedge lies remembrance and melancholy, so I sit and try to draw the memories more firmly around me. The house has grown very cold, and the silence is like a distant roar.

• Snap out of it! — turn to 2367

## 2367

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

I have a clear enough conception of my miseries and situation, if that is what you mean. I have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me. I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. But I perceive that all this is mere vexation of spirit. Snap out of it, you tell me? I see everything clearly now. There is no meaning, no purpose, no God. Our hopes and dreams are cruel shadows, distracting us from the awful realization that this is an empty life, a hollow life, to which reason can only respond with despair.

A bitten moon shines down, softly blurred by a smoky autumn mist that has wiped out all but the brightest stars. The grass has the silvery sheen of an impending frost. No wind disturbs the leafless shrubbery.

I am standing in the middle of the lawn. My feet are bare and wet, and the cold is seeping up through my body like sap in a tree. I'm shivering, but that will pass. In a short time, the cold will give way to numbness. Then a warmth which some have described as pleasant. What sensation follows warmth, no one has ever come back to tell. The moment of oblivion, like the moment of falling asleep, is a discovery that leaves no trace in the mind.

• If you kill yourself, your enemy has won. — turn to 2375

You're right. This slow descent into hopelessness is only what my adversary wants. I must remember who I am. The squalor in which I have allowed myself to sink, and the despair that has crept into my soul, are among the self-wrongs that Marcus Aurelius cautions us against. Whatever befalls a man, his victory or his defeat are not in the hands of others but stem from within.

My reason, which has slept in hibernation through the long scourging winter of horrors, now wakens in the warmth of hatred. These misfortunes have one cause - the monster I created, the miserable daemon I sent abroad into the world for my destruction. Thinking of [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: him]], I rise from my chair and throw open the curtains. A low sun slants blindingly into the room from a sky like a wall of ice. I feel my rage uncurl like a blossom in the light. In the darkness, *there* is my beacon: the monster's destruction. I will, I *will* have [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_demonize: it in my grasp. And when I do, I'll wreak a great and signal revenge on its]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_demonize: him in my grasp. And when I do, I'll wreak a great and signal revenge on his]] cursed head.

I have formed in my heart a resolution to pursue my enemy, and this purpose quietens my agony. Every time I rise from sleep, when dream's tranquillity melts away and the harsh pieces of reality slot back into place, my first thought is to take my razor and have an end to all of it. But first I must erase the stain that I have left on the world. I will extirpate that prodigy of evil, even at the cost of my own life - indeed, my life having now become intolerable to me, the only consideration is to ensure our mutual destruction.

Having made this resolution, the hurricane of my feelings has given way to calm. I summon lawyers, arranging for sums of money to be sent for later collection at banks across Europe - for I have no doubt that my hunt for the monster could carry me to the ends of the earth. For day-to-day expenses I have a few jewels that belonged to my mother.

I must plan. My mind is my one advantage over [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the monster]] and I must use it to fullest advantage. Then there is the question of whether I should do this alone. I have means. I am the head of one of Geneva's most prestigious families. Should I enlist aid in my endeavours?

• Yes, if you can. — turn to 2420
• No, you can't trust anyone else. — turn to 2500

Is this killing myself, then? I stand here. I could move. The tremors of cold are passing, but I could still turn around and walk back into the house. I say it to you, I think it, it would be that easy. But I don't do it. I stand here as the frost crackles underfoot. In the morning, they will find me, and -

A fox emerges from the bushes. He's hesitant. He must sense something, but I am motionless, so whatever danger tickles the hair of his neck at this moment cannot come from me. Not making a sound, he glides nearer.

Right in front of me now. Curious, not afraid. His eyes are occasional lambent flickers in the darkness.

I move. All it takes is for my hand to rise a few inches. He reacts at once - but not as a prey animal would, not with a start. He veers away as gracefully as if it were already his purpose, across the lawn swift and silent as an arrow, slipping into the night.

It's enough. I don't believe in signs, but I have seen the shoulder of Orion. I turn and walk back into the house, choosing to live for another day.

I will extirpate that prodigy of evil, even at the cost of my own life - indeed, my life having now become intolerable to me, the only consideration is to ensure our mutual destruction.

Having made this resolution, the hurricane of my feelings has given way to calm. I summon lawyers, arranging for sums of money to be sent for later collection at banks across Europe - for I have no doubt that my hunt for the monster could carry me to the ends of the earth. For day-to-day expenses I have a few jewels that belonged to my mother.

I must plan. My mind is my one advantage over [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the monster]] and I must use it to fullest advantage. Then there is the question of whether I should do this alone. I have means. I am the head of one of Geneva's most prestigious families. Should I enlist aid in my endeavours?

• Yes, if you can. — turn to 2419
• No, you can't trust anyone else. — turn to 2499

## 2409
*(01_RB · Trust thread 2)*

My heart shrinks from telling you. He believed that I killed Elizabeth because I couldn't stand to be with a woman. And - oh my God, and that Henri and I were lovers. And, most dreadful of all, that Henri may have murdered my little brother. I can't... I can't...

Father, how could you believe this? This is madness! This is more monstrous than the truth! Hasn't our family borne enough horror, that you should concoct such vileness to adorn it?

Oh, but it was my own brew of guilt and secrecy that nourished such chimeric suspicions. And so I brought my beloved father to the most terrible end of all - haunted by a grotesque mistrust of his devoted son, he had only this left to him! Let the fire have this note. I only wish I could burn it from my memory.

→ Turn to 2362.

## 2414
*(01_RD · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

> Delete the keyword KW_demonize if you have it.

There is a criminal judge in the town, a man who knew my father. I go to see him, saying that I have an accusation to make. He wants to express his condolences, but I brush all that aside. Now that I have thrown off my torpor, I must keep going forward.

'I know what destroyed my family. Who, I should say. They were murdered - my brother and my father. I know the killer, and I demand that you do everything in your power to apprehend him.'

The magistrate hears all this with a look of serious attention. 'All of Geneva was shocked by your wife's death. Be assured, sir, I shan't spare any effort to catch the villain.'

'Good. I have a deposition to make, and I want you to hear it. Though let me say first, by way of warning, that it may be hard for you to believe so strange a tale.'

'Speak freely. I have learned to listen to the man as much as to his statement. When the truth is spoken, however strange the facts, there is something in the heart of it that compels belief.'

• Tell him everything. — turn to 2422
• Reveal just enough of the facts to make him believe you. — turn to 2462

'I know what destroyed my family. Who, I should say. They were murdered - my brother and my father. I know the killer, and I demand that you do everything in your power to apprehend him.'

The magistrate hears all this with a look of serious attention. 'All of Geneva was shocked by your wife's death. Be assured, sir, I shan't spare any effort to catch the villain.'

'Good. I have a deposition to make, and I want you to hear it. Though let me say first, by way of warning, that it may be hard for you to believe so strange a tale.'

'Speak freely. I have learned to listen to the man as much as to his statement. When the truth is spoken, however strange the facts, there is something in the heart of it that compels belief.'

## 2422
*(01_RE · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'You will soon see that my story is too coherent to be mistaken for a delusion. And I have no motive for lying.'

My manner as I thus address him is impressive but calm. I have enough previous experience to know that I must present my case in a way that doesn't allow him to dismiss it as a lunatic's raving. I tell him everything, giving all the dates, all of the bare facts, as dispassionately as I can.

At first the judge seems entirely incredulous, but as I continue he becomes more interested. He sits forward in his chair. At some points in the narrative I see him shudder with horror. At others he is quietly attentive, his expression unmarred by disbelief.

'This is the nature of being whom I accuse,' I conclude. 'He must be hunted down, captured and punished. It is your duty as a magistrate and as a man to help me obtain justice for my murdered family.'

## 2430
*(01_RF · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I jump to my feet. 'It's evident that nothing I say will make you understand. My revenge is of no moment to you. A vice it may be, but it is the devouring and only passion of my soul. My rage is unspeakable when I reflect that the murderer, whom I turned loose upon society, still exists. You refuse my just demand. I have but one resource. I devote myself, either in my life or death, to his destruction.'

I am trembling as I say this. There is a frenzy in my manner and something of that ferocity which the martyrs of old are said to have possessed. But to a Genevan magistrate, whose mind is occupied by ideas other than those of devotion and heroism, my state of mind must seem like madness.

He adopts a soothing tone, as a nurse does to a child, and refers to my recent bereavement.

'Man,' I cry, 'you don't know how ignorant you are! Do you think I am a halfwit? Cease[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -3: , imbecile]] - you know not what it is you say.'

I break from the house, angry and disturbed, and pace the streets as I meditate on some other course of action.

• And what do you decide? — turn to 2494

'Eight feet tall! And grotesquely misshapen. It would be hard to mistake him for the average burglar.'

'Even without necessarily understanding everything you've told me, Doctor Frankenstein, I accept there is a dangerous murderer at large. ## 2454
*(01_RI · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'I would willingly afford you every aid in your pursuit,' he says, and I'm aware of the jarring contrast between his mildness and my vehemence. 'But the creature of whom you speak appears to have powers that would thwart my best exertions. Who can follow an animal which can traverse the sea of ice, and inhabit caves and dens where no man would venture to intrude?'

My heart sinks. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < 1: Despite having seemed to listen to my tale and to give it fair credence, his tone tells me that he does not believe a word.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ 1: It's obvious he intends to do nothing.]]

'Besides,' he continues, 'one of the crimes took place almost two years ago, the other several months. The killer could be halfway to the Orient by now.'

'I have no doubt that he remains near at hand. And if he has indeed taken refuge in the Alps, he may be hunted like the chamois, and destroyed as a beast of prey. But I perceive your thoughts - you do not credit my narrative, and do not intend to pursue my enemy with the punishment which is his desert.' As I speak, I feel the rage burning in my face.

'You are mistaken,' he says, a little intimidated. 'I will exert myself. If it is in my power to seize - well, the monster, if we must call him that - be assured that he shall suffer punishment proportionate to his crimes. But I fear, from what you have yourself described to be his abilities, that this will prove impossible. You must make up your mind to disappointment.'

• He's just humouring you. — turn to 2430

## 2462
*(01_RJ · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I weave him a story about a homicidal madman whom I treated in Paris as part of my studies, a hulking brute of a man with terrible disfigurements that set him apart from humanity. It has the beauty of being much the truth, though without the constructed body parts and the vitalizing spark through clay-like flesh. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: That's usually where I lose my listeners, I've found.]]

'He was an inmate at Charenton, where he fell under the influence of the Marquis de Sade. Thus his brutality was refined into cruelty.'

'And this man escaped?'

[[If Empathy > 5, read the following:]]

I cast a sharp look over his shoulder and see him twitch nervously. Good, so he believes me.

'During the Revolution. Of course, all my attempts to civilize him with a serene environment were undone. He emerged into a bloodbath. Everywhere around him, shops were being smashed and looted, people torn apart by mobs. Violence, it must have seemed to him, had become the proper order of things.'

'And you say this man - '

'I prefer to say monster.'

'Yes, a monster indeed. And he has made himself the nemesis of your family?'

'He blames me for offering him a life of peace and goodness, in contrast to everything he witnessed after his escape.'

• This is good. He believes you. — turn to 2470
• It's hopeless. Only you can kill the monster. — turn to 2478

## 2470
*(01_RK · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'I shall arrange protection for you,' says the magistrate decisively. 'I only wish you had come to me sooner. Your wife might still be alive.'

'Protection? No, no - we need to hunt him down.'

He purses his lips, and I feel a twinge of anger at his complacency. 'My dear sir, when he comes to assault you, as he surely will, my men will be ready.'

'How many men?'

'Two... Three.' He nods. 'An adequate number.'

'He has the strength of ten men. A hail of bullets might not stop him. He ignores pain, needs no rest, and he has a lifetime in which to exact his retribution on me. Lying in wait for him is futile. He must be hunted down.'

I see the look in his eyes. I've gone too far. I'm losing him.

'A hail of bullets?' He shakes his head as if to clear it. 'And how can I hunt him? Where is he? I don't have the manpower to scour the whole countryside. Surely if we wait...'

'I don't have that long.'

He says nothing, only looks at me quizzically. How can I tell him that my anger would run out? I must attack to survive, I need to fuel my anger. When it is gone I will have nothing left.

• This is a waste of time. — turn to 2486

'I shall arrange protection for you,' says the magistrate decisively. 'I only wish you had come to me sooner. Your wife might still be alive.'

'Protection? No, no - we need to hunt him down.'

He purses his lips, and I feel a twinge of anger at his complacency. 'My dear sir, when he comes to assault you, as he surely will, my men will be ready.'

'How many men?'

'Two... Three.' He nods. 'An adequate number.'

'He has the strength of ten men. A hail of bullets might not stop him. He ignores pain, needs no rest, and he has a lifetime in which to exact his retribution on me. Lying in wait for him is futile. He must be hunted down.'

I see the look in his eyes. I've gone too far. I'm losing him.

'A hail of bullets?' He shakes his head as if to clear it. 'And how can I hunt him? Where is he? I don't have the manpower to scour the whole countryside. Surely if we wait...'

'I don't have that long.'

He says nothing, only looks at me quizzically. How can I tell him that my anger would run out? I must attack to survive, I need to fuel my anger. When it is gone I will have nothing left.

• This is a waste of time. — turn to 2490

## 2478
*(01_RL · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

> Note the keyword KW_f_two_9.

'I don't think you can help me,' I tell him.

'Then who could?' He folds his hands. 'What help do you want?'

'Mountaineers, trackers, dogs, men with guns. If he is among the Alps, we must find his lair and trap him. If he is hiding in the countryside, or even in some deserted dwelling within the city, we must search until we find him. He must be surrounded. It will take many men. He could even be in the lake.'

'What?' The magistrate blinks, gives me a tiny half-smile. 'You mean he might have drowned himself?'

'He could remain underwater for hours at a time. I'm not sure. I didn't study him enough, but I think so.'

'It's October. Rather cold for a man to live like a fish.'

'He's indifferent to discomfort. It would have to freeze before he would notice.'

Somewhere I went too far. His look is hardened, incredulous. 'I can set a man to watch your house,' he offers.

'That would be useless,' I say, rising to take my leave. 'I would simply have yet another death on my conscience.'

• You need to come up with a better plan. — turn to 2494

## 2486
*(01_RM · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I rise to take my leave. 'You cannot help me,' I say.

He nods. 'I don't think I can. I'm sorry, Frankenstein.'

What slip have I made that makes him think me mad? It must be an excess of vehemence, or perhaps something in the eyes. Men who went up Olympus would be driven from their home villages, pelted with stones, cast out. Truth and madness have the same look.

Despite the outcome of the meeting, I emerge into the street with freshened spirits for what is to come. It feels as if the last chains have been cast away. Before it was brute against civilized man. Now I understand that I am an outcast too. There is nothing left that can stop me from destroying him.

## 2494
*(01_RN · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

As long as I remain in one place, my enemy controls the circumstances of our struggle. He can dictate the moment and place of his attacks, and [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_f_two_9: as I told the magistrate]]he could pick from a dozen hiding places inaccessible to me.

So I consider his disadvantages. I take a pen and list them. He may be reluctant to kill me, because [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: I am the only being to whom he has any attachment in the world]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 0: I am the only one who knows how to create more like him]]. His deformity creates two problems. First, it means that he must forage for or steal his food. Even though he needs little sustenance, that costs him time and effort. Second, he must find it hard to disguise his presence among men, making it hard to travel freely during the day.

He is physically robust, but he cannot turn to a physician for treatment if he is injured[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_b_eleven_4: , as illustrated by his account of being shot by the woodsman]]. And injury becomes more likely when he is forced to travel, to risk discovery, and to accommodate himself to different climates and terrains.

Therefore I conclude that by harrying him from place to place, I can deprive him of the best of his resources, and so gain the upper hand.

• And if he decides to stand and fight? — turn to 2502
• Then you may be leaving your homeland forever. — turn to 2510

## 2501
*(01_RN · Trust thread 6 to 9)*

As long as I remain in one place, my enemy controls the circumstances of our struggle. He can dictate the moment and place of his attacks, and [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_f_two_9: as I told the magistrate]]he could pick from a dozen hiding places inaccessible to me.

So I consider his disadvantages. I take a pen and list them. He may be reluctant to kill me, because [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy > 0: I am the only being to whom he has any attachment in the world]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≤ 0: I am the only one who knows how to create more like him]]. His deformity creates two problems. First, it means that he must forage for or steal his food. Even though he needs little sustenance, that costs him time and effort. Second, he must find it hard to disguise his presence among men, making it hard to travel freely during the day.

He is physically robust, but he cannot turn to a physician for treatment if he is injured[[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_b_eleven_4: , as illustrated by his account of being shot by the woodsman]]. And injury becomes more likely when he is forced to travel, to risk discovery, and to accommodate himself to different climates and terrains.

Therefore I conclude that by harrying him from place to place, I can deprive him of the best of his resources, and so gain the upper hand.

• And if he decides to stand and fight? — turn to 2509
• Then you may be leaving your homeland forever. — turn to 2517

I hardly need to tell you I have no greater hopes than that.

## 2510
*(01_RP · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

Before I leave, knowing that I am unlikely ever to return here, there is something I must do. I am at the cemetery where Elizabeth, my father and my brother repose. It is late afternoon. The red and yellow leaves lie in deep rustling drifts and a few gritty specks of snow hang in the air, making it seem as though reality's canvas is beginning to crack.

By previous arrangement, the sexton has left the mausoleum gate unlocked for me. Inside is echoing silence. A few leaves have been blown inside on the white marble where generations of my family trod, their names now listed on the walls like so many books filed in a library never again to be read.

Without intending to, I find myself kneeling before the recess where they were lately laid to rest. A few skeletal flowers protrude from a vase - unreplenished in the weeks I spent sunk in melancholy. There should be a ritual, something to mark this final threshold I'm about to cross. I bow my head to the floor. The stone is cold on my lips.

'By the sacred earth on which I kneel, by the shades that wander near me, by the deep and eternal grief that I feel, I swear.' The words come effortlessly, without requiring thought, as though I'm reciting a formula that I've always known. 'And by thee, O Night, and by the spirits that preside over thee, I swear to pursue the demon who caused this misery until he or I shall perish in mortal conflict. For this purpose I will preserve my life. To execute this dear revenge I will again behold the sun and tread the earth, which otherwise should vanish from my eyes forever. And I call on you spirits of the dead, and on you wandering ministers of vengeance, to aid me in my work. Let the cursed and hellish monster drink deep of agony. Let him feel the despair that now torments me.'

• Do you speak in anger? — turn to 2518
• Or would you say you are coldly determined? — turn to 2526

## 2534
*(01_RS · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I begin my vow with solemnity, and an awe that almost assures me that the shades of my murdered friends hear and approve, but the furies possess me as I conclude. Rage chokes my final words into an inchoate howl.

I've been here longer than I intended. Outside, the sun has set and the shadows have rushed in among the stones. The outlines of the tombs against the dimming sky resemble a sunken ruin.

As I look, the gate swings shut. I watch, I don't try to stop it. A heavy cloaked figure is there, silhouetted against the last of the light. He slips the chain through the bars of the gate and I hear the snap of the padlock. Yellow eyes stare from that face that is as devoid of expression as a mask.

'Do you come here to remember the days of darkness, Frankenstein?'

'Vile insect. Tattered thing. Release me and I shall put an end to you.'

'And that is why you have not put an end to yourself. I heard your vow.' He laughs. 'You did not, in former days, believe in goblins and spirits.'

'I believe in vengeance, monster - that only. If you heard me speak just now to those, your victims, who lie here, that is because I am dead too, but cannot make the journey until I have set right the atrocity I committed those years ago.'

'The crime of giving me life?'

• 'Yes.' — turn to 2550
• 'Not that only.' — turn to 2558

## 2540
*(01_RS · Trust thread 5)*

I begin my vow with solemnity, and an awe that almost assures me that the shades of my murdered friends hear and approve, but the furies possess me as I conclude. Rage chokes my final words into an inchoate howl.

I've been here longer than I intended. Outside, the sun has set and the shadows have rushed in among the stones. The outlines of the tombs against the dimming sky resemble a sunken ruin.

As I look, the gate swings shut. I watch, I don't try to stop it. A heavy cloaked figure is there, silhouetted against the last of the light. He slips the chain through the bars of the gate and I hear the snap of the padlock. Yellow eyes stare from that face that is as devoid of expression as a mask.

'Do you come here to remember the days of darkness, Frankenstein?'

## 2550
*(01_RV · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'So you are like a man who finds a savage lion in a cage and throws the door open for its escape?'

'Precisely so. And all the lives it takes are my fault.'

'You would not blame the lion.'

'It's in a lion's nature to kill,' I say before I realize he has trapped me twice over, with words as well as bars.

'I am hated for doing monstrous things. Why? I was created a monster, was I not? You created me thus.'

'I created a man. You've made yourself a monster.'

'I think I have acted out your secret desires, Frankenstein. Which makes you the monster pretending to be a man.'

With a harsh laugh, he turns and lopes swiftly away through the gathering dusk. Locked inside the vault, I can only put my hands to the bars and watch him go.

• Call for help. — turn to 2590

## 2558
*(01_RW · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'No, it was much more, wasn't it? The act of creation cannot be evil. Your crime was in spurning what you had made, casting me out alone into the world without hope or knowledge.'

'I don't deny it. But I have been punished merely for a mistake - the oversight of callow youth.'

'If you think your punishment unjust, Frankenstein, how much more is mine. Once I had dreams of virtue and happiness. Once I hoped to meet with others who, pardoning my outward deformity, would love me for the excellent qualities that I was capable of bringing forth. I was nourished with high thoughts of honour and devotion. But now vice has degraded me beneath the meanest animal. No crime, no mischief, no malignity, no misery, can be found comparable to mine. When I call over the frightful catalogue of my deeds, I cannot believe that I am he whose thoughts were once filled with sublime and transcendent visions of the beauty and the majesty of goodness. But it is so - the fallen angel becomes a malignant devil. Yet even Satan had friends and associates in his desolation. I am alone, I am content to suffer alone, and when I die I am well satisfied to be remembered as a monster.'

• Why indulge him by listening to this? — turn to 2566
• He need not have chosen to be a monster. — turn to 2574

I was nourished with high thoughts of honour and devotion. But now vice has degraded me beneath the meanest animal. No crime, no mischief, no malignity, no misery, can be found comparable to mine. When I call over the frightful catalogue of my deeds, I cannot believe that I am he whose thoughts were once filled with sublime and transcendent visions of the beauty and the majesty of goodness. But it is so - the fallen angel becomes a malignant devil. Yet even Satan had friends and associates in his desolation. I am alone, I am content to suffer alone, and when I die I am well satisfied to be remembered as a monster.'

• Why indulge him by listening to this? — turn to 2573
• He need not have chosen to be a monster. — turn to 2581

## 2574
*(01_RY · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'I made you with free will. If you are a monster, it's because you decided to be one.'

There is a grating of metal on stone as he tenses his grip on the gate. I am conscious that he could tear it from its hinges as I might break a twig from a tree. When he speaks, there is the extra edge of fury in his guttural voice.

'I tried to be a man! When I first sought the sympathy of my fellow man, it was because I wished to share the love of virtue, the feelings of happiness and affection with which my whole being overflowed. But now virtue has become to me a shadow, and happiness and affection are turned into bitter and loathing despair, in what should I seek for sympathy?

'I told you my story, but I could not sum up the hours and months of misery I endured. I desired love and fellowship, and I was spurned. Was there no injustice in this? Am I to be thought the only monster, when all humankind sinned against me? Why don't you hate Felix, whom I helped in his adversity but who drove me away? [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_b_eleven_4: Why not blame the rustic who rewarded me with a bullet for saving his lover's life?]]No, you do not consider those virtuous and immaculate beings to be in any way culpable. It is I, miserable and abandoned, who am an abortion to be spurned and kicked at and trampled on.'[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < 0:

'I have ceased to think of you as a sentient being of any kind. To me you are like a fire, out of control, that must be extinguished.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ 0:

'It is too late to speak to me of loss of innocence, demon. You have forfeited that right and, because the blood on your hands is also on mine, I have devoted my existence to your destruction.]]'

He pauses for a long time, seeming to reflect deeply, before saying. 'Yes, it's fitting. To the end, then. To our last breaths.'

He turns and lopes swiftly away through the gathering dusk. Locked inside the vault, I can only put my hands to the bars and watch the object of my hatred flee from sight.

• Call for help. — turn to 2590
• Someone will come to let you out at dawn. — turn to 2598

## 2582
*(01_RZ · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I am answered through the stillness of the late afternoon by a loud and fiendish laugh. It rings heavily on my ears, the galleries of the surrounding charnels re-echo it, and I feel as if all hell surrounds me with mockery. Surely in this moment I should be possessed by frenzy, and destroy my miserable existence - except my vow was heard, and so I am reserved for vengeance.

The laughter dies away. I look up at the doorway but see only the grey, exsanguined sky and the deep tide of shadow that has crept among the tombs. Then a well-known and abhorred voice, distorted to an echo by the walls of the vault so that it apparently emanates from close to my ear, addresses me in an audible whisper: 'I am satisfied, miserable wretch. You have determined to live, and I am satisfied.'

I am on my feet and darting towards the door, but he is faster. A heavy cloaked shape tips into view, as big and unstoppable as a boulder, and slams the gate before I can reach it. I hear the snap of the padlock.

'Devil!'

I catch a glimpse of his yellow eyes in the twilight. 'If you had wisdom, Frankenstein, you would stay there and rot among your ancestors. But instead you will pursue me, because you do not realize that you are already dead.'

He turns and lopes away, despite his lopsided gait, with more than mortal speed. I can only put my hands to the bars and watch the object of my hatred flee from sight.

• Call for help. — turn to 2590
• Someone will come to let you out at dawn. — turn to 2598

I am on my feet and darting towards the door, but he is faster. A heavy cloaked shape tips into view, as big and unstoppable as a boulder, and slams the gate before I can reach it. I hear the snap of the padlock.

'Devil!'

I catch a glimpse of his yellow eyes in the twilight. 'If you had wisdom, Frankenstein, you would stay there and rot among your ancestors. But instead you will pursue me, because you do not realize that you are already dead.'

He turns and lopes away, despite his lopsided gait, with more than mortal speed. I can only put my hands to the bars and watch the object of my hatred flee from sight.

I am answered through the stillness of the late afternoon by a loud and fiendish laugh. It rings heavily on my ears, the galleries of the surrounding charnels re-echo it, and I feel as if all hell surrounds me with mockery. Surely in this moment I should be possessed by frenzy, and destroy my miserable existence - except my vow was heard, and so I am reserved for vengeance.

The laughter dies away. I look up at the doorway but see only the grey, exsanguined sky and the deep tide of shadow that has crept among the tombs. ## 2592
*(01_S0 · Trust thread 1)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

I don't have to shout for long. The sexton's assistant, an old man who digs and tends the common graves, comes shuffling along the gallery outside. He has no lantern. The interior of the vault is in complete darkness now. He must only be able to see me as a dim outline.

'The wind blew the gate shut,' I tell him, mainly to give him the reassurance of hearing my voice.

'And locked it, sir?' He's doubtful, but in a moment I hear him fumbling with the keys.

'Did you see anyone else?' I ask as he opens the gate for me.

'No one comes here at this hour, sir. No living soul.'

**END OF CHAPTER ONE**

## 2598
*(01_S1 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

The knights of old used to begin their lives of chivalry with a vigil before the altar. My own purpose is grimmer, but the rite will serve. I kneel not before God, but before the angry host of ancestors whose name has been stained with innocent blood. In the dark of the night I hear them whispering to me. I know what I must do.

Before dawn I hear the sweep of a broom among the dry dead leaves that have drifted in along the charnel gallery. The sexton's assistant gives a start when he sees me, then hurries to fetch the keys.

The morning air off the mountains holds that deeper cold that says winter is coming. I stand in the pale dawn, breathing the sharp air, remade by my vigil for the long ordeal that lies ahead.

**END OF CHAPTER ONE**

• CHAPTER TWO — turn to 2606

## 2606
*(01_S3 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

[ILLUSTRATION: pic6_2.jpg]

**CHAPTER TWO**
*Encompassed by Peril*

I pursue him for months. Guided by a slight clue, I first follow the windings of the Rhône, then a trail that takes me through northern Italy. I seek him along the fog-shrouded canals of Venice as autumn turns to winter, and down the Adriatic, sailing into the slate-coloured Ionian Sea past the cliffs where Penelope watched for her husband to return. I bow my head in bitterness, knowing there is no hearth swept for my homecoming. At the end of this chase, I will leave my bones in a strange land.

In Athens I find evidence that my quarry has been there just before me: a packet left with the banker who is to release me funds. It's a scrap of butcher's paper, clumsily tied with string. The banker tells me it was left in the doorway of his office after business hours. The handwriting, I notice, is not unlike my own. Of course, he has my notebook to copy from.

## 2614
*(01_S4 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

A lady's white glove with a rusty red stain on the cuff. He snapped Elizabeth's neck, so I doubt it's her blood. The glove, though - I didn't go through her belongings after the murder. It could be hers.

'I'm sorry, sir,' says the banker, backing out of his own office. 'I'll give you some privacy.'

I'm weeping. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -2: I curse my own weakness.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ -2: I hadn't noticed.]] The thought of him having taken this and carrying it with him across Europe seems as gross a violation as any of his crimes so far.

As I leave the banker's offices, it occurs to me that we are in a bustling city. The busiest city that my search has so far brought me to. It cannot have been easy for the monster to find a hiding place here. Yet he must have done - close enough to the city, at any rate, to be able to deliver the package by dead of night.

A lady's white glove with a rusty red stain on the cuff. He snapped Elizabeth's neck, so I doubt it's her blood. The glove, though - I didn't go through her belongings after the murder. It could be hers.

'I'm sorry, sir,' says the banker, backing out of his own office. 'I'll give you some privacy.'

I'm weeping. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -2: I curse my own weakness.]][[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy ≥ -2: I hadn't noticed.]] The thought of him having taken this and carrying it with him across Europe seems as gross a violation as any of his crimes so far.

As I leave the banker's offices, it occurs to me that we are in a bustling city. The busiest city that my search has so far brought me to. It cannot have been easy for the monster to find a hiding place here. Yet he must have done - close enough to the city, at any rate, to be able to deliver the package by dead of night.

• Perhaps a cemetery? — turn to 2633
• A hospital? — turn to 2649
• The Parthenon? — turn to 2641
• It's pointless to look. He will have moved on. — turn to 2665

'It is a practical joke by a friend,' I explain. 'Now, sir, if I may have my money...'

## 2630
*(01_S7 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I waste several days visiting the graveyards of Athens. I find nothing to suggest the monster was here. In one patch of ground behind a small church there is a headstone marked LAVENZA. It is overgrown with weeds like the rest, but there are a few fresh flowers on the grave. However, it would be a mistake to read anything into that.

• Then it's time to move on. — turn to 2662

## 2638
*(01_S8 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

'It's a steep climb,' a would-be dragoman tells me, offering to carry my pack. His speech is a mixture of French and English, a necessary hedging of bets for one in his profession.

He must be surprised to see me ascend the steps so nimbly. 'We Swiss find going uphill easier than a level road,' I call back.

I don't know what I expect to find. The old ruins are dingier than I expected, a sad sight under the grey winter sky, though the marble reliefs of horses and heroes still convey a patina of awe. For some reason I'm reminded of my father, though I don't believe he knew Pericles from a periwinkle.

What clue would my foe leave me here? A message under a rock? There are hundreds, and nothing to stop sightseers taking them away in their pockets. I even see a plump, smug-faced young Englishman walking around with several Ottoman officials, who seem quite happy to stand back while he removes a few pieces of stone with a chisel.

• The monster isn't here. It's time to move on. — turn to 2662

## 2646
*(01_S9 · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I call on some teaching hospitals where they might store cadavers for dissection. It is illegal under the Ottoman rule, of course, but physicians have a way of getting around that in all parts of the world. Distributing a little money brings me to a mortuary attendant who is still shaken by the experience of finding one of his bodies walking around in the middle of the night.

A clever ploy on [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: my enemy]]'s part, I suppose - hiding in plain sight. But although it boosts my morale to have discovered one of his stratagems, the practical value is nil. He is long gone.

• Perhaps he had another reason for hiding here? — turn to 2654
• You're wasting time here. — turn to 2662

> Note the keyword KW_f_four_7.

You could be onto something. I seek out one of the professors. Lacking a common modern tongue, we fall back on Latin. He tells me that several volumes were stolen from the hospital's library.

'When?'

'Very recently. Three days ago.'

That was around the time the mortuary attendant saw a flayed cadaver walking past his door. 'And the books that were taken?'

'Recent works on surgery, French and English for the most part. I was going to have them translated.'

Interesting. Why would [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: my monster]] want to study such things? With a sense of foreboding, I return to the hotel to plan the next stage of my journey.

## 2662
*(01_SC · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I track him to Istanbul, where some beggars are talking of a huge cloaked figure haunting the docks at night. Scouring the waterfront on both sides of the city, I have found nothing the past few nights, but the sightings continue, so I believe he is still here.

Yes, see there on the hawser of that ship? Just keep walking. There, hanging halfway up the cable, a bundle like a fat spider wound in its web. That's him. Do you think he saw me? Tomorrow I shall take passage on that ship, wherever it is bound.

Each day, as we sail east, I make a thorough search of the ship. Where can he hide himself? I find no trace, but food is stolen from the kitchen - more than rats would take. He is aboard and yet somehow he evades me when we dock at Sevastopol.

Into the wilds of Tartary and Russia, then. He stays ahead of me, but he cannot shake me off. I am learning how to follow his tracks. And he has the disadvantage of alienness - sometimes the peasants, scared by a horrid apparition, tell me where he's gone. But he cannot stay away from habitation altogether, for I am driving him north where it is harder to find food in the wild. The snows descend, and I see the print of his huge step on the white plain. Look at my footprint beside it. Look at that. Yet the giant runs, and I pursue.

• You're not chasing him. He's luring you. — turn to 2670
• You'll struggle to survive in the north too. — turn to 2678

## 2670
*(01_SD · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

It's not so straightforward as you suppose. The pattern you have perceived has another explanation, you see - namely that we are *both* guided by a spirit, who moves us like chess pieces towards the inevitable end. Oh, but I am so weary. The weariness has got into my bones and it gnaws at them. When will my guiding spirit see fit to conduct me to the demon, so that I can destroy him and take the rest I so desire?

Or, as you see it, must I die and he yet live? If I do, swear to me that he shall not escape, that you will satisfy my vengeance. Perhaps I should not ask you to undertake my crusade. No, I'm not so selfish as that. Forget I spoke.[[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < -1: I have no grounds in any case for thinking you'd keep a promise made to me.]]

Yet, when I am dead, if he should appear, if the ministers of vengeance should conduct him to you, swear that he shall not live - swear that he shall not triumph over my accumulated woes, and live to make another as wretched as I am. Beware, he is eloquent and persuasive, and once his words even had power over my heart. Don't trust him. Don't listen to him. His soul is as hellish as his form, full of treachery and fiendish malice. Harden your heart and stop your ears if he tries to coerce you. Think of William, Justine, Henri, Elizabeth, my father, and of the wretched Victor, and thrust your sword into his heart. I will hover near and direct the steel aright.

• It's unlucky to talk of failure. — turn to 2686
• Be resolute. You will strike that blow yourself. — turn to 2709

His soul is as hellish as his form, full of treachery and fiendish malice. Harden your heart and stop your ears if he tries to coerce you. Think of William, Justine, Henri, Elizabeth, my father, and of the wretched Victor, and thrust your sword into his heart. I will hover near and direct the steel aright.

## 2678
*(01_SE · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

Cold, hunger, and fatigue are the least of my pains. I am cursed by some devil, and carry about with me a private and eternal hell. Although - do you know, I feel that a spirit of good follows and directs my steps. How else have I stayed on the fiend's trail? There have been a score of times I thought I'd lost him, and then a clue was revealed to me as if by providence.

And it's not just the help of strangers - the sightings of a monstrous figure, the reports of stolen food and clothes. The spirit helps me in the wild too. Take yesterday. I had been unable to sleep, and after stalking a deer for miles through the frosty woods, my gun misfired and it got away from me. I could have sunk to the ground there and expired of fatigue and hunger. But I found a rock on which a repast was laid out for me. Look, I wrapped up some of it and I'll make my supper of it shortly. It's just plain fare, as you can see. The sort of coarse meal the peasants of this country eat. But what manna to a starving traveller!

Remember the vow I took in the mausoleum? I mustn't doubt that this food was set there by the spirits that I invoked then to aid me. Often, when all there is around is this sere wilderness, and the heavens cloudless, and I am parched by thirst, a slight cloud bedims the sky, sheds the few drops I need to revive me, and vanishes.

Why are you looking at me like that? This food is sent by the spirits, I tell you. You believe that, don't you?

• Yes. — turn to 2701
• No. — turn to 2694

## 2709
*(01_SJ · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I follow the courses of rivers when I can, so as to have fresh water and fish to hand when I cannot find villages to trade at. I brought money with me, and gain the friendship of the villagers by distributing either that or game that I have snared. In return I can usually find shelter and a hearth to sleep at, in the early stages of our chase at least. But those settlements that lie along the rivers are the very reason that the demon I pursue generally avoids them. His habitat is the wild, so it must be mine too.

As we penetrate further north, human habitation becomes sparse. Now I seldom see another soul from one day to the next, and must subsist on the wild animals that cross my path. I have little time for hunting, though. The monster needs less food, you see, and I cannot allow the weakness of my appetites and mortal frailty to delay me. Today my head aches with hunger, and each mile feels like a league, but I must press on.

• Why is he heading north? What's the reason? — turn to 2716
• You need to gather some food. — turn to 2740

## 2710
*(01_SJ · Trust thread 0 to 1)*

I follow the courses of rivers when I can, so as to have fresh water and fish to hand when I cannot find villages to trade at. I brought money with me, and gain the friendship of the villagers by distributing either that or game that I have snared. In return I can usually find shelter and a hearth to sleep at, in the early stages of our chase at least. But those settlements that lie along the rivers are the very reason that the demon I pursue generally avoids them. His habitat is the wild, so it must be mine too.

As we penetrate further north, human habitation becomes sparse. Now I seldom see another soul from one day to the next, and must subsist on the wild animals that cross my path. I have little time for hunting, though. The monster needs less food, you see, and I cannot allow the weakness of my appetites and mortal frailty to delay me. Today my head aches with hunger, and each mile feels like a league, but I must press on.

• Why is he heading north? What's the reason? — turn to 2717

## 2716
*(01_SK · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

You wonder as to the feelings of my quarry? How am I to know? He leaves me signs - sometimes taunting messages cut into stone or wood, like this one carved in the bark of a tree. It hasn't started to heal over. Not more than two days old, I'd say.

'My reign is not yet over.' That's definitely what he's written. It's unfortunate that he was exposed to Milton at an impressionable age.

Ah, and an arrow pointing to another inscription on this tree: 'You live, and my power is complete.' And yet another arrow, pointing I suppose to that next tree there. Yes, look - the bark has definitely been cut away.

He could have scattered these lurid little epigrams through the whole forest. I would do better to spend a few hours in hunting than follow this paper chase of messages.

Here he has written, 'Follow me. I seek the everlasting ices of the north...' and it continues on this tree, '... where you will feel the misery of cold and frost to which I am impassive.'

His purpose in leaving this is to sap my morale. It won't work. I know he is stronger, but I am cleverer and more determined. Are you sure the message is worth deciphering? Well, there's another part of it here: 'Come on, enemy. We have yet to wrestle for our lives.'

Wrestle nothing, I have a brace of pistols, a musket and a nine-inch knife to even up our fight. Let him come to wrestle me. I'll blow his kneecaps off first. Another part of it here: 'Many hard and miserable hours must you endure until that period shall arrive.'

This is foolish! These messages could stretch to the Arctic Circle, and his intent is only to mock me.

• You're right, hunt for food instead. — turn to 2743

## 2737
*(01_SP · Trust thread 4)*

Now this is interesting. 'If you follow not too tardily...'

Quickly, to the next tree. Ah. Look at this. You were right to make me read it all:

'... You will find near this place a dead hare. Eat and be refreshed.'

And here it is, in the hollow of the next tree, cut up and wind-dried and neatly parcelled in leaves stitched together with pine needles. Quite a little picnic. He's nicely solicitous of my welfare, the fiend I created.

It's not much of a meal. No matter. It is enough to sustain me for another day. [[!! EDIT inline, if Empathy < 0: This and hate are all I need.]]

As I continue north, the snows thicken and the cold grows harder to bear. At least I now have a sledge and dogs, bought with the last of my mother's jewels, so I am making better ground. Days can go by without me seeing anyone. The peasants are shut up in their huts, firewood piled deep against the walls, roofs humped with snow. Few enough animals to be seen now, even though it must be spring in warmer climes. I still need to hunt, though - I can ignore my own hunger, but not the dogs'. Fish would be easiest, but the ice on the rivers is too thick.

Do you see that on the horizon? Like a great gleaming plain? It's the ocean. It must be frozen solid - look, you can only tell it from the land by its rugged desolation. There is a desert harsher than any of Arabia, my friend. An empty quarter indeed. And fathoms of water churning under that trackless ice. Out on that and you're lost to history. I can't imagine returning.

• It's a good sign, that frozen sea. — turn to 2748
• You'll leave your bones out there. — turn to 2754
• Do you think you're gaining on the monster? — turn to 2759

## 2746
*(01_ST · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

It is.

I'll tell you why. In the harsh country we've come through, where food is scarce, [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: the monster]]'s need for less sustenance has helped him. But out there, there's nothing. I'll have the supplies I can pack on the sledge. If the worst comes to the worst, I can feed one dog to the others. But [[!! EDIT inline, if you have KW_adom: Adom]][[!! EDIT inline, if you do not have KW_adom: my foe]] will find no game, no vegetation. Nothing to eat. I'll harry him until he withers, drive him till his frame is blackened by the scalding cold. *That's* why the ocean is a good sign. The Greeks wept for joy when they beheld the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, and hailed with rapture the boundary of their toils. I do not weep, but I will kneel down here and, with a full heart, thank my guiding spirit for bringing me to the battleground on which I can destroy my enemy.

Keeping the frozen ocean ever ahead, in two days I reach a hamlet on the shore. The inhabitants must have heard my dogs but remain stubbornly indoors. I crunch through the snow and knock on the door of the largest cabin, hoping it is a store where I can buy fuel and provisions. I catch a face at the window. After a minute the door opens a crack, releasing a waft of warm steamy air.

I've learned a few words. 'Food. Also wood. Oil. A bed tonight.'

It's getting late, though you would hardly know it from the eternally pale sky. Better to rest here and go on tomorrow.

The door opens wider and an old woman tugs me inside, jabbering angrily about - I assume - the loss of heat. The first thing I notice is the stink of pipe tobacco. My eyes adjust to the gloom and I see several men seated around a spitting, cracking pine fire. They turn away when they see me looking. The woman points to a stool and goes into the next room. The smell of cooking gives me some hope that she has understood.

• These rustics dislike strangers. Best keep your distance. — turn to 2762
• Talk to them. They may have seen the monster. — turn to 2766

> !! TRUST-DEPENDENT TEXT: this copy of the section reads differently from its other Trust-thread copies (text or links that today depend on Trust have been resolved for this thread).

I fear you may be right. I must now commence a destructive and almost endless journey across the mountainous ice - in cold that few of the natives of this land can long endure, and which I, used to a genial climate, cannot hope to survive.

But, no. I won't allow myself to think this way. The idea that the fiend should be triumphant - it makes my blood boil, it makes my pulse hammer in my chest. The heat of righteous anger must sustain me. And I have my constant companions, the spirits of the dead, hovering round and urging me onwards. I'll endure, whatever you may say.

Keeping the frozen ocean ever ahead, in two days I reach a hamlet on the shore. The inhabitants must have heard my dogs but remain stubbornly indoors. I crunch through the snow and knock on the door of the largest cabin, hoping it is a store where I can buy fuel and provisions. I catch a face at the window. After a minute the door opens a crack, releasing a waft of warm steamy air.

I've learned a few words. 'Food. Also wood. Oil. A bed tonight.'

It's getting late, though you would hardly know it from the eternally pale sky. Better to rest here and go on tomorrow.

The door opens wider and an old woman tugs me inside, jabbering angrily about - I assume - the loss of heat. The first thing I notice is the stink of pipe tobacco. My eyes adjust to the gloom and I see several men seated around a spitting, cracking pine fire. They turn away when they see me looking. The woman points to a stool and goes into the next room. The smell of cooking gives me some hope that she has understood.

• These rustics dislike strangers. Best keep your distance. — turn to 2763
• Talk to them. They may have seen the monster. — turn to 2768

## 2757
*(01_SW · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

I believe so. He might have a sledge himself, but his size counts against him. He'd need more dogs to pull it, and that's more mouths to feed. I am sure that, just as I was losing ground before, I'm gaining on him now. I don't believe he can be more than one day's journey ahead. ## 2762
*(01_SY · Trust thread -7 to -1)*

Have no fear on that score; I have learned that it's wiser to stay aloof, keep silent, and show them as little money as possible. I have previously set aside a few coins, which I make a play of handing over with great reluctance when the old woman comes back with a plate of black bread and beetroot stew. Actually, I hardly need to pretend, as I'm down to the bottom of my purse and my fingers are so stiff with cold that it's hard to count them out anyway. I have enough for provisions, and I'll need to exchange my land sledge for one better suited to the frozen ocean. Other than that, I have no more use for money now.

It's a labour to eat the stew. I'm so weary. But I must - it could be the last good meal I have for a while, and I need the energy. The fire is so hot. The smoke makes my eyes raw.

The old woman is standing in front of me. She's asking me a question. What's that in her hand? A folded piece of paper. My first thought is that it must have dropped from my pocket, as the writing looks like my hand. But it's his. He's been here, and he left me a letter.

I nod and take it from her, aware of the hostile looks this earns me from the men around the hearth. There's fear as well as anger in their muttering. No doubt the fiend terrorized their village, took what he wanted, and went on across the frozen sea. I want to tell them I'm not like that, I'm not with him. But I don't speak their language, and in any case it wouldn't be true.

• Are you going to read the letter? — turn to 2774
